nodes.title: Passage 4
nodes.content: While argparse is the default recommended standard library module for implementing basic command line applications, authors with more exacting requirements for exactly how their command line applications behave may find it doesn’t provide the necessary level of control. Refer to Choosing an argument parsing library for alternatives to consider when argparse doesn’t support behaviors that the application requires (such as entirely disabling support for interspersed options and positional arguments, or accepting option parameter values that start with - even when they correspond to another defined option).

nodes.title: Passage 7
nodes.content: The argparse module makes it easy to write user-friendly command-line interfaces. The program defines what arguments it requires, and argparse will figure out how to parse those out of sys.argv . The argparse module also automatically generates help and usage messages. The module will also issue errors when users give the program invalid arguments.

nodes.title: Passage 58
nodes.content: Sometimes, several parsers share a common set of arguments. Rather than repeating the definitions of these arguments, a single parser with all the shared arguments and passed to parents= argument to ArgumentParser can be used. The parents= argument takes a list of ArgumentParser objects, collects all the positional and optional actions from them, and adds these actions to the ArgumentParser object being constructed:

ArgumentParser ( parents = [ parent_parser ]) >>> foo_parser . add_argument ( 'foo' ) >>> foo_parser . parse_args ([ '--parent' , '2' , 'XXX' ]) Namespace(foo='XXX', parent=2) >>> bar_parser = argparse . ArgumentParser ( parents = [ parent_parser ]) >>> bar_parser . add_argument ( '--bar' ) >>> bar_parser . parse_args ([ '--bar' , 'YYY' ]) Namespace(bar='YYY', parent=None)

nodes.title: Passage 84
nodes.content: Sometimes, when dealing with a particularly long argument list, it may make sense to keep the list of arguments in a file rather than typing it out at the command line. If the fromfile_prefix_chars= argument is given to the ArgumentParser constructor, then arguments that start with any of the specified characters will be treated as files, and will be replaced by the arguments they contain. For example:

ArgumentParser ( fromfile_prefix_chars = '@' ) >>> parser . add_argument ( '-f' ) >>> parser . parse_args ([ '-f' , 'foo' , '@args.txt' ]) Namespace(f='bar')

nodes.content: The parse_args() method attempts to give errors whenever the user has clearly made a mistake, but some situations are inherently ambiguous. For example, the command-line argument -1 could either be an attempt to specify an option or an attempt to provide a positional argument. The parse_args() method is cautious here: positional arguments may only begin with - if they look like negative numbers and there are no options in the parser that look like negative numbers:

nodes.title: Passage 323
nodes.content: Many programs split up their functionality into a number of subcommands, for example, the svn program can invoke subcommands like svn checkout , svn update , and svn commit . Splitting up functionality this way can be a particularly good idea when a program performs several different functions which require different kinds of command-line arguments. ArgumentParser supports the creation of such subcommands with the add_subparsers() method. The add_subparsers() method is normally called with no arguments and returns a special action object. This object has a single method, add_parser() , which takes a command name and any ArgumentParser constructor arguments, and returns an ArgumentParser object that can be modified as usual.

nodes.title: Passage 7
nodes.content: This module defines functions and classes which implement a flexible event logging system for applications and libraries.

nodes.title: Passage 8
nodes.content: The key benefit of having the logging API provided by a standard library module is that all Python modules can participate in logging, so your application log can include your own messages integrated with messages from third-party modules.

nodes.title: Passage 9
nodes.content: Here’s a simple example of idiomatic usage:

nodes.title: Passage 10
nodes.content: # myapp.py import logging import mylib logger = logging . getLogger ( __name__ ) def main (): logging . basicConfig ( filename = 'myapp.log' , level = logging . INFO ) logger . info ( 'Started' ) mylib . do_something () logger . info ( 'Finished' ) if __name__ == '__main__' : main ()

nodes.title: Passage 11
nodes.content: # mylib.py import logging logger = logging . getLogger ( __name__ ) def do_something (): logger . info ( 'Doing something' )

nodes.title: Passage 12
nodes.content: If you run myapp.py , you should see this in myapp.log :

nodes.title: Passage 13
nodes.content: INFO:__main__:Started INFO:mylib:Doing something INFO:__main__:Finished

nodes.title: Passage 14
nodes.content: The key feature of this idiomatic usage is that the majority of code is simply creating a module level logger with getLogger(__name__) , and using that logger to do any needed logging. This is concise, while allowing downstream code fine-grained control if needed. Logged messages to the module-level logger get forwarded to handlers of loggers in higher-level modules, all the way up to the highest-level logger known as the root logger; this approach is known as hierarchical logging.

nodes.title: Passage 15
nodes.content: For logging to be useful, it needs to be configured: setting the levels and destinations for each logger, potentially changing how specific modules log, often based on command-line arguments or application configuration. In most cases, like the one above, only the root logger needs to be so configured, since all the lower level loggers at module level eventually forward their messages to its handlers. basicConfig() provides a quick way to configure the root logger that handles many use cases.

nodes.title: Passage 16
nodes.content: The module provides a lot of functionality and flexibility. If you are unfamiliar with logging, the best way to get to grips with it is to view the tutorials ( see the links above and on the right ).

nodes.title: Passage 17
nodes.content: The basic classes defined by the module, together with their attributes and methods, are listed in the sections below.

nodes.title: Passage 18
nodes.content: Loggers expose the interface that application code directly uses.

nodes.title: Passage 19
nodes.content: Handlers send the log records (created by loggers) to the appropriate destination.

nodes.title: Passage 20
nodes.content: Filters provide a finer grained facility for determining which log records to output.

nodes.title: Passage 21
nodes.content: Formatters specify the layout of log records in the final output.

nodes.title: Passage 23
nodes.content: Loggers have the following attributes and methods. Note that Loggers should NEVER be instantiated directly, but always through the module-level function logging.getLogger(name) . Multiple calls to getLogger() with the same name will always return a reference to the same Logger object.

nodes.title: Passage 24
nodes.content: The name is potentially a period-separated hierarchical value, like foo.bar.baz (though it could also be just plain foo , for example). Loggers that are further down in the hierarchical list are children of loggers higher up in the list. For example, given a logger with a name of foo , loggers with names of foo.bar , foo.bar.baz , and foo.bam are all descendants of foo . In addition, all loggers are descendants of the root logger. The logger name hierarchy is analogous to the Python package hierarchy, and identical to it if you organise your loggers on a per-module basis using the recommended construction logging.getLogger(__name__) . That’s because in a module, __name__ is the module’s name in the Python package namespace.

nodes.title: Passage 44
nodes.content: If this attribute evaluates to true, events logged to this logger will be passed to the handlers of higher level (ancestor) loggers, in addition to any handlers attached to this logger. Messages are passed directly to the ancestor loggers’ handlers - neither the level nor filters of the ancestor loggers in question are considered.

nodes.title: Passage 46
nodes.content: Spelling it out with an example: If the propagate attribute of the logger named A.B.C evaluates to true, any event logged to A.B.C via a method call such as logging.getLogger('A.B.C').error(...) will [subject to passing that logger’s level and filter settings] be passed in turn to any handlers attached to loggers named A.B , A and the root logger, after first being passed to any handlers attached to A.B.C . If any logger in the chain A.B.C , A.B , A has its propagate attribute set to false, then that is the last logger whose handlers are offered the event to handle, and propagation stops at that point.

nodes.title: Passage 49
nodes.content: If you attach a handler to a logger and one or more of its ancestors, it may emit the same record multiple times. In general, you should not need to attach a handler to more than one logger - if you just attach it to the appropriate logger which is highest in the logger hierarchy, then it will see all events logged by all descendant loggers, provided that their propagate setting is left set to True . A common scenario is to attach handlers only to the root logger, and to let propagation take care of the rest.

nodes.content: setLevel ( level )

nodes.title: Passage 62
nodes.content: Sets the threshold for this logger to level . Logging messages which are less severe than level will be ignored; logging messages which have severity level or higher will be emitted by whichever handler or handlers service this logger, unless a handler’s level has been set to a higher severity level than level .

nodes.title: Passage 63
nodes.content: When a logger is created, the level is set to NOTSET (which causes all messages to be processed when the logger is the root logger, or delegation to the parent when the logger is a non-root logger). Note that the root logger is created with level WARNING .

nodes.title: Passage 64
nodes.content: The term ‘delegation to the parent’ means that if a logger has a level of NOTSET, its chain of ancestor loggers is traversed until either an ancestor with a level other than NOTSET is found, or the root is reached.

nodes.title: Passage 65
nodes.content: If an ancestor is found with a level other than NOTSET, then that ancestor’s level is treated as the effective level of the logger where the ancestor search began, and is used to determine how a logging event is handled.

nodes.title: Passage 66
nodes.content: If the root is reached, and it has a level of NOTSET, then all messages will be processed. Otherwise, the root’s level will be used as the effective level.

nodes.title: Passage 67
nodes.content: See Logging Levels for a list of levels.

nodes.title: Passage 68
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.2: The level parameter now accepts a string representation of the level such as ‘INFO’ as an alternative to the integer constants such as INFO . Note, however, that levels are internally stored as integers, and methods such as e.g. getEffectiveLevel() and isEnabledFor() will return/expect to be passed integers.

nodes.content: debug ( msg , * args , ** kwargs )

nodes.title: Passage 85
nodes.content: Logs a message with level DEBUG on this logger. The msg is the message format string, and the args are the arguments which are merged into msg using the string formatting operator. (Note that this means that you can use keywords in the format string, together with a single dictionary argument.) No % formatting operation is performed on msg when no args are supplied.

nodes.title: Passage 86
nodes.content: There are four keyword arguments in kwargs which are inspected: exc_info , stack_info , stacklevel and extra .

nodes.title: Passage 87
nodes.content: If exc_info does not evaluate as false, it causes exception information to be added to the logging message. If an exception tuple (in the format returned by sys.exc_info() ) or an exception instance is provided, it is used; otherwise, sys.exc_info() is called to get the exception information.

nodes.title: Passage 88
nodes.content: The second optional keyword argument is stack_info , which defaults to False . If true, stack information is added to the logging message, including the actual logging call. Note that this is not the same stack information as that displayed through specifying exc_info : The former is stack frames from the bottom of the stack up to the logging call in the current thread, whereas the latter is information about stack frames which have been unwound, following an exception, while searching for exception handlers.

nodes.title: Passage 89
nodes.content: You can specify stack_info independently of exc_info , e.g. to just show how you got to a certain point in your code, even when no exceptions were raised. The stack frames are printed following a header line which says:

nodes.title: Passage 90
nodes.content: Stack (most recent call last):

nodes.title: Passage 91
nodes.content: This mimics the Traceback (most recent call last): which is used when displaying exception frames.

nodes.title: Passage 92
nodes.content: The third optional keyword argument is stacklevel , which defaults to 1 . If greater than 1, the corresponding number of stack frames are skipped when computing the line number and function name set in the LogRecord created for the logging event. This can be used in logging helpers so that the function name, filename and line number recorded are not the information for the helper function/method, but rather its caller. The name of this parameter mirrors the equivalent one in the warnings module.

nodes.title: Passage 93
nodes.content: The fourth keyword argument is extra which can be used to pass a dictionary which is used to populate the __dict__ of the LogRecord created for the logging event with user-defined attributes. These custom attributes can then be used as you like. For example, they could be incorporated into logged messages. For example:

nodes.title: Passage 94
nodes.content: FORMAT = ' %(asctime)s %(clientip)-15s %(user)-8s %(message)s ' logging . basicConfig ( format = FORMAT ) d = { 'clientip' : '192.168.0.1' , 'user' : 'fbloggs' } logger = logging . getLogger ( 'tcpserver' ) logger . warning ( 'Protocol problem: %s ' , 'connection reset' , extra = d )

nodes.title: Passage 95
nodes.content: would print something like

nodes.title: Passage 96
nodes.content: 2006-02-08 22:20:02,165 192.168.0.1 fbloggs Protocol problem: connection reset

nodes.title: Passage 97
nodes.content: The keys in the dictionary passed in extra should not clash with the keys used by the logging system. (See the section on LogRecord attributes for more information on which keys are used by the logging system.)

nodes.title: Passage 98
nodes.content: If you choose to use these attributes in logged messages, you need to exercise some care. In the above example, for instance, the Formatter has been set up with a format string which expects ‘clientip’ and ‘user’ in the attribute dictionary of the LogRecord . If these are missing, the message will not be logged because a string formatting exception will occur. So in this case, you always need to pass the extra dictionary with these keys.

nodes.title: Passage 99
nodes.content: While this might be annoying, this feature is intended for use in specialized circumstances, such as multi-threaded servers where the same code executes in many contexts, and interesting conditions which arise are dependent on this context (such as remote client IP address and authenticated user name, in the above example). In such circumstances, it is likely that specialized Formatter s would be used with particular Handler s.

nodes.content: The logging module is intended to be thread-safe without any special work needing to be done by its clients. nodes.title: Passage 392
nodes.content: Provides an overriding level level for all loggers which takes precedence over the logger’s own level. When the need arises to temporarily throttle logging output down across the whole application, this function can be useful. Its effect is to disable all logging calls of severity level and below, so that if you call it with a value of INFO, then all INFO and DEBUG events would be discarded, whereas those of severity WARNING and above would be processed according to the logger’s effective level. If logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) is called, it effectively removes this overriding level, so that logging output again depends on the effective levels of individual loggers.

nodes.title: Passage 2
nodes.content: The decimal module provides support for fast correctly rounded decimal floating-point arithmetic. It offers several advantages over the float datatype:
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 3
nodes.content: Decimal “is based on a floating-point model which was designed with people in mind, and necessarily has a paramount guiding principle – computers must provide an arithmetic that works in the same way as the arithmetic that people learn at school.” – excerpt from the decimal arithmetic specification.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 4
nodes.content: Decimal numbers can be represented exactly. In contrast, numbers like 1.1 and 2.2 do not have exact representations in binary floating point. End users typically would not expect 1.1 + 2.2 to display as 3.3000000000000003 as it does with binary floating point.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 5
nodes.content: The exactness carries over into arithmetic. In decimal floating point, 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 - 0.3 is exactly equal to zero. In binary floating point, the result is 5.5511151231257827e-017 . While near to zero, the differences prevent reliable equality testing and differences can accumulate. For this reason, decimal is preferred in accounting applications which have strict equality invariants.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 6
nodes.content: The decimal module incorporates a notion of significant places so that 1.30 + 1.20 is 2.50 . The trailing zero is kept to indicate significance. This is the customary presentation for monetary applications. For multiplication, the “schoolbook” approach uses all the figures in the multiplicands. For instance, 1.3 * 1.2 gives 1.56 while 1.30 * 1.20 gives 1.5600 .
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 7
nodes.content: Unlike hardware based binary floating point, the decimal module has a user alterable precision (defaulting to 28 places) which can be as large as needed for a given problem:
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 8
nodes.content: >>> from decimal import * >>> getcontext () . prec = 6 >>> Decimal ( 1 ) / Decimal ( 7 ) Decimal('0.142857') >>> getcontext () . prec = 28 >>> Decimal ( 1 ) / Decimal ( 7 ) Decimal('0.1428571428571428571428571429')
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 9
nodes.content: Both binary and decimal floating point are implemented in terms of published standards. While the built-in float type exposes only a modest portion of its capabilities, the decimal module exposes all required parts of the standard. When needed, the programmer has full control over rounding and signal handling. This includes an option to enforce exact arithmetic by using exceptions to block any inexact operations.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 10
nodes.content: The decimal module was designed to support “without prejudice, both exact unrounded decimal arithmetic (sometimes called fixed-point arithmetic) and rounded floating-point arithmetic.” – excerpt from the decimal arithmetic specification.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 11
nodes.content: The module design is centered around three concepts: the decimal number, the context for arithmetic, and signals.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 12
nodes.content: A decimal number is immutable. It has a sign, coefficient digits, and an exponent. To preserve significance, the coefficient digits do not truncate trailing zeros. Decimals also include special values such as Infinity , -Infinity , and NaN . The standard also differentiates -0 from +0 .
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 13
nodes.content: The context for arithmetic is an environment specifying precision, rounding rules, limits on exponents, flags indicating the results of operations, and trap enablers which determine whether signals are treated as exceptions. Rounding options include ROUND_CEILING , ROUND_DOWN , ROUND_FLOOR , ROUND_HALF_DOWN , ROUND_HALF_EVEN , ROUND_HALF_UP , ROUND_UP , and ROUND_05UP .
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 14
nodes.content: Signals are groups of exceptional conditions arising during the course of computation. Depending on the needs of the application, signals may be ignored, considered as informational, or treated as exceptions. The signals in the decimal module are: Clamped , InvalidOperation , DivisionByZero , Inexact , Rounded , Subnormal , Overflow , Underflow and FloatOperation .
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 15
nodes.content: For each signal there is a flag and a trap enabler. When a signal is encountered, its flag is set to one, then, if the trap enabler is set to one, an exception is raised. Flags are sticky, so the user needs to reset them before monitoring a calculation.

nodes.title: Passage 657
nodes.content: The number system for the decimal module provides special values including NaN , sNaN , -Infinity , Infinity , and two zeros, +0 and -0 .
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 658
nodes.content: Infinities can be constructed directly with: Decimal('Infinity') . Also, they can arise from dividing by zero when the DivisionByZero signal is not trapped. Likewise, when the Overflow signal is not trapped, infinity can result from rounding beyond the limits of the largest representable number.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 659
nodes.content: The infinities are signed (affine) and can be used in arithmetic operations where they get treated as very large, indeterminate numbers. For instance, adding a constant to infinity gives another infinite result.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 660
nodes.content: Some operations are indeterminate and return NaN , or if the InvalidOperation signal is trapped, raise an exception. For example, 0/0 returns NaN which means “not a number”. This variety of NaN is quiet and, once created, will flow through other computations always resulting in another NaN . This behavior can be useful for a series of computations that occasionally have missing inputs — it allows the calculation to proceed while flagging specific results as invalid.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 661
nodes.content: A variant is sNaN which signals rather than remaining quiet after every operation. This is a useful return value when an invalid result needs to interrupt a calculation for special handling.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 662
nodes.content: The behavior of Python’s comparison operators can be a little surprising where a NaN is involved. A test for equality where one of the operands is a quiet or signaling NaN always returns False (even when doing Decimal('NaN')==Decimal('NaN') ), while a test for inequality always returns True . An attempt to compare two Decimals using any of the < , <= , > or >= operators will raise the InvalidOperation signal if either operand is a NaN , and return False if this signal is not trapped. Note that the General Decimal Arithmetic specification does not specify the behavior of direct comparisons; these rules for comparisons involving a NaN were taken from the IEEE 854 standard (see Table 3 in section 5.7). To ensure strict standards-compliance, use the compare() and compare_signal() methods instead.

nodes.title: Passage 663
nodes.content: The signed zeros can result from calculations that underflow. They keep the sign that would have resulted if the calculation had been carried out to greater precision. Since their magnitude is zero, both positive and negative zeros are treated as equal and their sign is informational.

nodes.title: Passage 698
nodes.content: Q: When does rounding occur in a computation?
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 699
nodes.content: A: It occurs after the computation. The philosophy of the decimal specification is that numbers are considered exact and are created independent of the current context. They can even have greater precision than current context. Computations process with those exact inputs and then rounding (or other context operations) is applied to the result of the computation:

nodes.title: Passage 701
nodes.content: Q: Some decimal values always print with exponential notation. Is there a way to get a non-exponential representation?
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 702
nodes.content: A: For some values, exponential notation is the only way to express the number of significant places in the coefficient. For example, expressing 5.0E+3 as 5000 keeps the value constant but cannot show the original’s two-place significance.

nodes.content: If an application does not care about tracking significance, it is easy to remove the exponent and trailing zeroes, losing significance, but keeping the value unchanged:

nodes.content: A: Yes, any binary floating-point number can be exactly expressed as a Decimal though an exact conversion may take more precision than intuition would suggest:

nodes.title: Passage 709
nodes.content: Q: Within a complex calculation, how can I make sure that I haven’t gotten a spurious result because of insufficient precision or rounding anomalies.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 710
nodes.content: A: The decimal module makes it easy to test results. A best practice is to re-run calculations using greater precision and with various rounding modes. Widely differing results indicate insufficient precision, rounding mode issues, ill-conditioned inputs, or a numerically unstable algorithm.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 711
nodes.content: Q: I noticed that context precision is applied to the results of operations but not to the inputs. Is there anything to watch out for when mixing values of different precisions?
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 712
nodes.content: A: Yes. The principle is that all values are considered to be exact and so is the arithmetic on those values. Only the results are rounded. The advantage for inputs is that “what you type is what you get”. A disadvantage is that the results can look odd if you forget that the inputs haven’t been rounded:
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 713
nodes.content: >>> getcontext () . prec = 3 >>> Decimal ( '3.104' ) + Decimal ( '2.104' ) Decimal('5.21') >>> Decimal ( '3.104' ) + Decimal ( '0.000' ) + Decimal ( '2.104' ) Decimal('5.20')
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 714
nodes.content: The solution is either to increase precision or to force rounding of inputs using the unary plus operation:
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 715
nodes.content: >>> getcontext () . prec = 3 >>> + Decimal ( '1.23456789' ) # unary plus triggers rounding Decimal('1.23')
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 716
nodes.content: Alternatively, inputs can be rounded upon creation using the Context.create_decimal() method:
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 717
nodes.content: >>> Context ( prec = 5 , rounding = ROUND_DOWN ) . create_decimal ( '1.2345678' ) Decimal('1.2345')
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 718
nodes.content: Q: Is the CPython implementation fast for large numbers?
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 719
nodes.content: A: Yes. In the CPython and PyPy3 implementations, the C/CFFI versions of the decimal module integrate the high speed libmpdec library for arbitrary precision correctly rounded decimal floating-point arithmetic [ 1 ] . libmpdec uses Karatsuba multiplication for medium-sized numbers and the Number Theoretic Transform for very large numbers.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 720
nodes.content: The context must be adapted for exact arbitrary precision arithmetic. Emin and Emax should always be set to the maximum values, clamp should always be 0 (the default). Setting prec requires some care.
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 721
nodes.content: The easiest approach for trying out bignum arithmetic is to use the maximum value for prec as well [ 2 ] :
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 722
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 723
nodes.content: For inexact results, MAX_PREC is far too large on 64-bit platforms and the available memory will be insufficient:
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 724
nodes.content: >>> Decimal ( 1 ) / 3 Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>" , line 1 , in <module> MemoryError
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 725
nodes.content: On systems with overallocation (e.g. Linux), a more sophisticated approach is to adjust prec to the amount of available RAM. Suppose that you have 8GB of RAM and expect 10 simultaneous operands using a maximum of 500MB each:
path: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

nodes.title: Passage 726
nodes.content: >>> import sys >>> >>> # Maximum number of digits for a single operand using 500MB in 8-byte words >>> # with 19 digits per word (4-byte and 9 digits for the 32-bit build): >>> maxdigits = 19 * (( 500 * 1024 ** 2 ) // 8 ) >>> >>> # Check that this works: >>> c = Context ( prec = maxdigits , Emax = MAX_EMAX , Emin = MIN_EMIN ) >>> c . traps [ Inexact ] = True >>> setcontext ( c ) >>> >>> # Fill the available precision with nines: >>> x = Decimal ( 0 ) . logical_invert () * 9 >>> sys . getsizeof ( x ) 524288112 >>> x + 2 Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>" , line 1 , in <module> decimal.Inexact : [<class 'decimal.Inexact'>]

nodes.title: Passage 727
nodes.content: In general (and especially on systems without overallocation), it is recommended to estimate even tighter bounds and set the Inexact trap if all calculations are expected to be exact.

nodes.title: Passage 3
nodes.content: This module offers classes representing filesystem paths with semantics appropriate for different operating systems. Path classes are divided between pure paths , which provide purely computational operations without I/O, and concrete paths , which inherit from pure paths but also provide I/O operations.

nodes.title: Passage 4
nodes.content: If you’ve never used this module before or just aren’t sure which class is right for your task, Path is most likely what you need. It instantiates a concrete path for the platform the code is running on.

nodes.title: Passage 5
nodes.content: Pure paths are useful in some special cases; for example:

nodes.title: Passage 6
nodes.content: If you want to manipulate Windows paths on a Unix machine (or vice versa). You cannot instantiate a WindowsPath when running on Unix, but you can instantiate PureWindowsPath .

nodes.title: Passage 7
nodes.content: You want to make sure that your code only manipulates paths without actually accessing the OS. In this case, instantiating one of the pure classes may be useful since those simply don’t have any OS-accessing operations.

nodes.title: Passage 8
nodes.content: See also

nodes.title: Passage 9
nodes.content: PEP 428 : The pathlib module – object-oriented filesystem paths.

nodes.title: Passage 10
nodes.content: See also

nodes.title: Passage 31
nodes.content: Pure path objects provide path-handling operations which don’t actually access a filesystem. There are three ways to access these classes, which we also call flavours :

nodes.title: Passage 33
nodes.content: class pathlib. PurePath ( * pathsegments )

nodes.title: Passage 34
nodes.content: A generic class that represents the system’s path flavour (instantiating it creates either a PurePosixPath or a PureWindowsPath ):

nodes.title: Passage 35
nodes.content: >>> PurePath ( 'setup.py' ) # Running on a Unix machine PurePosixPath('setup.py')

nodes.title: Passage 36
nodes.content: Each element of pathsegments can be either a string representing a path segment, or an object implementing the os.PathLike interface where the __fspath__() method returns a string, such as another path object:

nodes.title: Passage 37
nodes.content: >>> PurePath ( 'foo' , 'some/path' , 'bar' ) PurePosixPath('foo/some/path/bar') >>> PurePath ( Path ( 'foo' ), Path ( 'bar' )) PurePosixPath('foo/bar')

nodes.title: Passage 38
nodes.content: When pathsegments is empty, the current directory is assumed:

nodes.title: Passage 39
nodes.content: >>> PurePath () PurePosixPath('.')

nodes.title: Passage 40
nodes.content: If a segment is an absolute path, all previous segments are ignored (like os.path.join() ):

nodes.title: Passage 41
nodes.content: >>> PurePath ( '/etc' , '/usr' , 'lib64' ) PurePosixPath('/usr/lib64') >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'c:/Windows' , 'd:bar' ) PureWindowsPath('d:bar')

nodes.title: Passage 42
nodes.content: On Windows, the drive is not reset when a rooted relative path segment (e.g., r'\foo' ) is encountered:

nodes.title: Passage 43
nodes.content: >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'c:/Windows' , '/Program Files' ) PureWindowsPath('c:/Program Files')

nodes.title: Passage 44
nodes.content: Spurious slashes and single dots are collapsed, but double dots ( '..' ) and leading double slashes ( '//' ) are not, since this would change the meaning of a path for various reasons (e.g. symbolic links, UNC paths):

nodes.title: Passage 45
nodes.content: >>> PurePath ( 'foo//bar' ) PurePosixPath('foo/bar') >>> PurePath ( '//foo/bar' ) PurePosixPath('//foo/bar') >>> PurePath ( 'foo/./bar' ) PurePosixPath('foo/bar') >>> PurePath ( 'foo/../bar' ) PurePosixPath('foo/../bar')

nodes.title: Passage 46
nodes.content: (a naïve approach would make PurePosixPath('foo/../bar') equivalent to PurePosixPath('bar') , which is wrong if foo is a symbolic link to another directory)

nodes.title: Passage 47
nodes.content: Pure path objects implement the os.PathLike interface, allowing them to be used anywhere the interface is accepted.

nodes.title: Passage 48
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.6: Added support for the os.PathLike interface.

nodes.content: class pathlib. PurePosixPath ( * pathsegments )

nodes.title: Passage 51
nodes.content: A subclass of PurePath , this path flavour represents non-Windows filesystem paths:

nodes.title: Passage 52

nodes.title: Passage 53
nodes.content: pathsegments is specified similarly to PurePath .

nodes.title: Passage 55
nodes.content: class pathlib. PureWindowsPath ( * pathsegments )

nodes.title: Passage 56
nodes.content: A subclass of PurePath , this path flavour represents Windows filesystem paths, including UNC paths :

nodes.title: Passage 57
nodes.content: >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'c:/' , 'Users' , 'Ximénez' ) PureWindowsPath('c:/Users/Ximénez') >>> PureWindowsPath ( '//server/share/file' ) PureWindowsPath('//server/share/file')

nodes.title: Passage 58
nodes.content: pathsegments is specified similarly to PurePath .

nodes.title: Passage 59
nodes.content: Regardless of the system you’re running on, you can instantiate all of these classes, since they don’t provide any operation that does system calls.

nodes.title: Passage 61
nodes.content: Paths are immutable and hashable . Paths of a same flavour are comparable and orderable. These properties respect the flavour’s case-folding semantics:

nodes.title: Passage 62
nodes.content: >>> PurePosixPath ( 'foo' ) == PurePosixPath ( 'FOO' ) False >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'foo' ) == PureWindowsPath ( 'FOO' ) True >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'FOO' ) in { PureWindowsPath ( 'foo' ) } True >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'C:' ) < PureWindowsPath ( 'd:' ) True

nodes.title: Passage 63
nodes.content: Paths of a different flavour compare unequal and cannot be ordered:

nodes.title: Passage 64
nodes.content: >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'foo' ) == PurePosixPath ( 'foo' ) False >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'foo' ) < PurePosixPath ( 'foo' ) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>" , line 1 , in <module> TypeError : '<' not supported between instances of 'PureWindowsPath' and 'PurePosixPath'

nodes.title: Passage 66
nodes.content: The slash operator helps create child paths, like os.path.join() . If the argument is an absolute path, the previous path is ignored. On Windows, the drive is not reset when the argument is a rooted relative path (e.g., r'\foo' ):

nodes.title: Passage 67
nodes.content: >>> p = PurePath ( '/etc' ) >>> p PurePosixPath('/etc') >>> p / 'init.d' / 'apache2' PurePosixPath('/etc/init.d/apache2') >>> q = PurePath ( 'bin' ) >>> '/usr' / q PurePosixPath('/usr/bin') >>> p / '/an_absolute_path' PurePosixPath('/an_absolute_path') >>> PureWindowsPath ( 'c:/Windows' , '/Program Files' ) PureWindowsPath('c:/Program Files')

nodes.title: Passage 68
nodes.content: A path object can be used anywhere an object implementing os.PathLike is accepted:

nodes.title: Passage 69
nodes.content: >>> import os >>> p = PurePath ( '/etc' ) >>> os . fspath ( p ) '/etc'

nodes.title: Passage 70
nodes.content: The string representation of a path is the raw filesystem path itself (in native form, e.g. with backslashes under Windows), which you can pass to any function taking a file path as a string:

nodes.title: Passage 71
nodes.content: >>> p = PurePath ( '/etc' ) >>> str ( p ) '/etc' >>> p = PureWindowsPath ( 'c:/Program Files' ) >>> str ( p ) 'c:\\Program Files'

nodes.title: Passage 72
nodes.content: Similarly, calling bytes on a path gives the raw filesystem path as a bytes object, as encoded by os.fsencode() :

nodes.title: Passage 73
nodes.content: >>> bytes ( p ) b'/etc'

nodes.title: Passage 74
nodes.content: Note

nodes.title: Passage 75
nodes.content: Calling bytes is only recommended under Unix. Under Windows, the unicode form is the canonical representation of filesystem paths.

nodes.title: Passage 77

nodes.title: Passage 81
nodes.content: >>> p = PurePath ( '/usr/bin/python3' ) >>> p . parts ('/', 'usr', 'bin', 'python3') >>> p = PureWindowsPath ( 'c:/Program Files/PSF' ) >>> p . parts ('c:\\', 'Program Files', 'PSF')

nodes.title: Passage 98

nodes.title: Passage 101
nodes.content: If the path starts with more than two successive slashes, PurePosixPath collapses them:

nodes.title: Passage 102

nodes.title: Passage 104
nodes.content: This behavior conforms to The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 6 , paragraph 4.11 Pathname Resolution :

nodes.title: Passage 105

nodes.content: PurePath. with_segments ( * pathsegments )

nodes.title: Passage 211
nodes.content: Create a new path object of the same type by combining the given pathsegments . This method is called whenever a derivative path is created, such as from parent and relative_to() . Subclasses may override this method to pass information to derivative paths, for example:

nodes.content: from pathlib import PurePosixPath class MyPath ( PurePosixPath ): def __init__ ( self , * pathsegments , session_id ): super () . __init__ ( * pathsegments ) self . session_id = session_id def with_segments ( self , * pathsegments ): return type ( self )( * pathsegments , session_id = self . session_id ) etc = MyPath ( '/etc' , session_id = 42 ) hosts = etc / 'hosts' print ( hosts . session_id ) # 42

nodes.title: Passage 215
nodes.content: Concrete paths are subclasses of the pure path classes. In addition to operations provided by the latter, they also provide methods to do system calls on path objects. There are three ways to instantiate concrete paths:

nodes.title: Passage 217
nodes.content: class pathlib. Path ( * pathsegments )

nodes.title: Passage 218
nodes.content: A subclass of PurePath , this class represents concrete paths of the system’s path flavour (instantiating it creates either a PosixPath or a WindowsPath ):

nodes.title: Passage 219
nodes.content: >>> Path ( 'setup.py' ) PosixPath('setup.py')

nodes.title: Passage 220
nodes.content: pathsegments is specified similarly to PurePath .

nodes.title: Passage 222
nodes.content: class pathlib. PosixPath ( * pathsegments )

nodes.title: Passage 223
nodes.content: A subclass of Path and PurePosixPath , this class represents concrete non-Windows filesystem paths:

nodes.title: Passage 224
nodes.content: >>> PosixPath ( '/etc/hosts' ) PosixPath('/etc/hosts')

nodes.title: Passage 225
nodes.content: pathsegments is specified similarly to PurePath .

nodes.title: Passage 226
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.13: Raises UnsupportedOperation on Windows. In previous versions, NotImplementedError was raised instead.

nodes.title: Passage 228
nodes.content: class pathlib. WindowsPath ( * pathsegments )

nodes.title: Passage 229
nodes.content: A subclass of Path and PureWindowsPath , this class represents concrete Windows filesystem paths:

nodes.title: Passage 230
nodes.content: >>> WindowsPath ( 'c:/' , 'Users' , 'Ximénez' ) WindowsPath('c:/Users/Ximénez')

nodes.title: Passage 231
nodes.content: pathsegments is specified similarly to PurePath .

nodes.title: Passage 232
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.13: Raises UnsupportedOperation on non-Windows platforms. In previous versions, NotImplementedError was raised instead.

nodes.title: Passage 233
nodes.content: You can only instantiate the class flavour that corresponds to your system (allowing system calls on non-compatible path flavours could lead to bugs or failures in your application):

nodes.title: Passage 234
nodes.content: >>> import os >>> os . name 'posix' >>> Path ( 'setup.py' ) PosixPath('setup.py') >>> PosixPath ( 'setup.py' ) PosixPath('setup.py') >>> WindowsPath ( 'setup.py' ) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>" , line 1 , in <module> File "pathlib.py" , line 798 , in __new__ % ( cls . __name__ ,)) UnsupportedOperation : cannot instantiate 'WindowsPath' on your system

nodes.title: Passage 235
nodes.content: Some concrete path methods can raise an OSError if a system call fails (for example because the path doesn’t exist).

nodes.title: Passage 237
nodes.content: Concrete path objects can be created from, and represented as, ‘file’ URIs conforming to RFC 8089 .

nodes.title: Passage 238
nodes.content: Note

nodes.title: Passage 239
nodes.content: File URIs are not portable across machines with different filesystem encodings .

nodes.title: Passage 328
nodes.content: Return True if the path is a mount point : a point in a file system where a different file system has been mounted. path: Comparison to the os and os.path modules

nodes.title: Passage 548
nodes.content: pathlib implements path operations using PurePath and Path objects, and so it’s said to be object-oriented . On the other hand, the os and os.path modules supply functions that work with low-level str and bytes objects, which is a more procedural approach. Some users consider the object-oriented style to be more readable.
path: Comparison to the os and os.path modules

nodes.title: Passage 549
nodes.content: Many functions in os and os.path support bytes paths and paths relative to directory descriptors . These features aren’t available in pathlib.
path: Comparison to the os and os.path modules

nodes.title: Passage 550
nodes.content: Python’s str and bytes types, and portions of the os and os.path modules, are written in C and are very speedy. pathlib is written in pure Python and is often slower, but rarely slow enough to matter.
path: Comparison to the os and os.path modules

nodes.title: Passage 551
nodes.content: pathlib’s path normalization is slightly more opinionated and consistent than os.path . For example, whereas os.path.abspath() eliminates “ .. ” segments from a path, which may change its meaning if symlinks are involved, Path.absolute() preserves these segments for greater safety.
path: Comparison to the os and os.path modules

nodes.title: Passage 552
nodes.content: pathlib’s path normalization may render it unsuitable for some applications:
path: Comparison to the os and os.path modules

nodes.title: Passage 553
nodes.content: pathlib normalizes Path("my_folder/") to Path("my_folder") , which changes a path’s meaning when supplied to various operating system APIs and command-line utilities. Specifically, the absence of a trailing separator may allow the path to be resolved as either a file or directory, rather than a directory only.
path: Comparison to the os and os.path modules

nodes.title: Passage 554
nodes.content: pathlib normalizes Path("./my_program") to Path("my_program") , which changes a path’s meaning when used as an executable search path, such as in a shell or when spawning a child process. Specifically, the absence of a separator in the path may force it to be looked up in PATH rather than the current directory.
path: Comparison to the os and os.path modules

nodes.title: Passage 555
nodes.content: As a consequence of these differences, pathlib is not a drop-in replacement for os.path .

nodes.title: Passage 2
nodes.content: SQLite is a C library that provides a lightweight disk-based database that doesn’t require a separate server process and allows accessing the database using a nonstandard variant of the SQL query language. Some applications can use SQLite for internal data storage. It’s also possible to prototype an application using SQLite and then port the code to a larger database such as PostgreSQL or Oracle.
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 3
nodes.content: The sqlite3 module was written by Gerhard Häring. It provides an SQL interface compliant with the DB-API 2.0 specification described by PEP 249 , and requires SQLite 3.15.2 or newer.

nodes.title: Passage 17
nodes.content: In this tutorial, you will create a database of Monty Python movies using basic sqlite3 functionality. It assumes a fundamental understanding of database concepts, including cursors and transactions .
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 18
nodes.content: First, we need to create a new database and open a database connection to allow sqlite3 to work with it. Call sqlite3.connect() to create a connection to the database tutorial.db in the current working directory, implicitly creating it if it does not exist:
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 19
nodes.content: import sqlite3 con = sqlite3 . connect ( "tutorial.db" )
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 20
nodes.content: The returned Connection object con represents the connection to the on-disk database.
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 21
nodes.content: In order to execute SQL statements and fetch results from SQL queries, we will need to use a database cursor. Call con.cursor() to create the Cursor :
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 22
nodes.content: cur = con . cursor ()
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 23
nodes.content: Now that we’ve got a database connection and a cursor, we can create a database table movie with columns for title, release year, and review score. For simplicity, we can just use column names in the table declaration – thanks to the flexible typing feature of SQLite, specifying the data types is optional. Execute the CREATE TABLE statement by calling cur.execute(...) :
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 24
nodes.content: cur . execute ( "CREATE TABLE movie(title, year, score)" )
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 25
nodes.content: We can verify that the new table has been created by querying the sqlite_master table built-in to SQLite, which should now contain an entry for the movie table definition (see The Schema Table for details). Execute that query by calling cur.execute(...) , assign the result to res , and call res.fetchone() to fetch the resulting row:
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 26
nodes.content: >>> res = cur . execute ( "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master" ) >>> res . fetchone () ('movie',)
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 27
nodes.content: We can see that the table has been created, as the query returns a tuple containing the table’s name. If we query sqlite_master for a non-existent table spam , res.fetchone() will return None :
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 28
nodes.content: >>> res = cur . execute ( "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE name='spam'" ) >>> res . fetchone () is None True
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 29
nodes.content: Now, add two rows of data supplied as SQL literals by executing an INSERT statement, once again by calling cur.execute(...) :
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 30
nodes.content: cur . execute ( """ INSERT INTO movie VALUES ('Monty Python and the Holy Grail', 1975, 8.2), ('And Now for Something Completely Different', 1971, 7.5) """ )
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 31
nodes.content: The INSERT statement implicitly opens a transaction, which needs to be committed before changes are saved in the database (see Transaction control for details). Call con.commit() on the connection object to commit the transaction:
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 32
nodes.content: con . commit ()
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 33
nodes.content: We can verify that the data was inserted correctly by executing a SELECT query. Use the now-familiar cur.execute(...) to assign the result to res , and call res.fetchall() to return all resulting rows:
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 34
nodes.content: >>> res = cur . execute ( "SELECT score FROM movie" ) >>> res . fetchall () [(8.2,), (7.5,)]
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 35
nodes.content: The result is a list of two tuple s, one per row, each containing that row’s score value.
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 36
nodes.content: Now, insert three more rows by calling cur.executemany(...) :
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 37
nodes.content: data = [ ( "Monty Python Live at the Hollywood Bowl" , 1982 , 7.9 ), ( "Monty Python's The Meaning of Life" , 1983 , 7.5 ), ( "Monty Python's Life of Brian" , 1979 , 8.0 ), ] cur . executemany ( "INSERT INTO movie VALUES(?, ?, ?)" , data ) con . commit () # Remember to commit the transaction after executing INSERT.
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 38
nodes.content: Notice that ? placeholders are used to bind data to the query. Always use placeholders instead of string formatting to bind Python values to SQL statements, to avoid SQL injection attacks (see How to use placeholders to bind values in SQL queries for more details).
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 39
nodes.content: We can verify that the new rows were inserted by executing a SELECT query, this time iterating over the results of the query:
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 40
nodes.content: >>> for row in cur . execute ( "SELECT year, title FROM movie ORDER BY year" ): ... print ( row ) (1971, 'And Now for Something Completely Different') (1975, 'Monty Python and the Holy Grail') (1979, "Monty Python's Life of Brian") (1982, 'Monty Python Live at the Hollywood Bowl') (1983, "Monty Python's The Meaning of Life")
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 41
nodes.content: Each row is a two-item tuple of (year, title) , matching the columns selected in the query.
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 42
nodes.content: Finally, verify that the database has been written to disk by calling con.close() to close the existing connection, opening a new one, creating a new cursor, then querying the database:
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 43
nodes.content: >>> con . close () >>> new_con = sqlite3 . connect ( "tutorial.db" ) >>> new_cur = new_con . cursor () >>> res = new_cur . execute ( "SELECT title, year FROM movie ORDER BY score DESC" ) >>> title , year = res . fetchone () >>> print ( f 'The highest scoring Monty Python movie is { title !r} , released in { year } ' ) The highest scoring Monty Python movie is 'Monty Python and the Holy Grail', released in 1975 >>> new_con . close ()
path: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases

nodes.title: Passage 44
nodes.content: You’ve now created an SQLite database using the sqlite3 module, inserted data and retrieved values from it in multiple ways.

nodes.content: detect_types ( int ) – Control whether and how data types not natively supported by SQLite are looked up to be converted to Python types, using the converters registered with register_converter() . Set it to any combination (using | , bitwise or) of PARSE_DECLTYPES and PARSE_COLNAMES to enable this. Column names take precedence over declared types if both flags are set. It is possible to override this behavior by specifying a _pack_ class attribute in the subclass definition. This must be set to a positive integer and specifies the maximum alignment for the fields. This is what #pragma pack(n) also does in MSVC. It is also possible to set a minimum alignment for how the subclass itself is packed in the same way #pragma align(n) works in MSVC. This can be achieved by specifying a _align_ class attribute in the subclass definition.

nodes.title: Passage 173
nodes.content: Behind the scenes, the pointer() function does more than simply create pointer instances, it has to create pointer types first. This is done with the POINTER() function, which accepts any ctypes type, and returns a new type:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 174
nodes.content: >>> PI = POINTER ( c_int ) >>> PI <class 'ctypes.LP_c_long'> >>> PI ( 42 ) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>" , line 1 , in <module> TypeError : expected c_long instead of int >>> PI ( c_int ( 42 )) <ctypes.LP_c_long object at 0x...> >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 175
nodes.content: Calling the pointer type without an argument creates a NULL pointer. NULL pointers have a False boolean value:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 176
nodes.content: >>> null_ptr = POINTER ( c_int )() >>> print ( bool ( null_ptr )) False >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 177
nodes.content: ctypes checks for NULL when dereferencing pointers (but dereferencing invalid non- NULL pointers would crash Python):
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 178
nodes.content: >>> null_ptr [ 0 ] Traceback (most recent call last): .... ValueError : NULL pointer access >>> >>> null_ptr [ 0 ] = 1234 Traceback (most recent call last): .... ValueError : NULL pointer access >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Type conversions
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 180
nodes.content: Usually, ctypes does strict type checking. This means, if you have POINTER(c_int) in the argtypes list of a function or as the type of a member field in a structure definition, only instances of exactly the same type are accepted. There are some exceptions to this rule, where ctypes accepts other objects. For example, you can pass compatible array instances instead of pointer types. So, for POINTER(c_int) , ctypes accepts an array of c_int:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 181
nodes.content: >>> class Bar ( Structure ): ... _fields_ = [( "count" , c_int ), ( "values" , POINTER ( c_int ))] ... >>> bar = Bar () >>> bar . values = ( c_int * 3 )( 1 , 2 , 3 ) >>> bar . count = 3 >>> for i in range ( bar . count ): ... print ( bar . values [ i ]) ... 1 2 3 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 182
nodes.content: In addition, if a function argument is explicitly declared to be a pointer type (such as POINTER(c_int) ) in argtypes , an object of the pointed type ( c_int in this case) can be passed to the function. ctypes will apply the required byref() conversion in this case automatically.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 183
nodes.content: To set a POINTER type field to NULL , you can assign None :
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 184
nodes.content: >>> bar . values = None >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 185
nodes.content: Sometimes you have instances of incompatible types. In C, you can cast one type into another type. ctypes provides a cast() function which can be used in the same way. The Bar structure defined above accepts POINTER(c_int) pointers or c_int arrays for its values field, but not instances of other types:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 186
nodes.content: >>> bar . values = ( c_byte * 4 )() Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>" , line 1 , in <module> TypeError : incompatible types, c_byte_Array_4 instance instead of LP_c_long instance >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 187
nodes.content: For these cases, the cast() function is handy.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 188
nodes.content: The cast() function can be used to cast a ctypes instance into a pointer to a different ctypes data type. cast() takes two parameters, a ctypes object that is or can be converted to a pointer of some kind, and a ctypes pointer type. It returns an instance of the second argument, which references the same memory block as the first argument:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 189
nodes.content: >>> a = ( c_byte * 4 )() >>> cast ( a , POINTER ( c_int )) <ctypes.LP_c_long object at ...> >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 190
nodes.content: So, cast() can be used to assign to the values field of Bar the structure:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 191
nodes.content: >>> bar = Bar () >>> bar . values = cast (( c_byte * 4 )(), POINTER ( c_int )) >>> print ( bar . values [ 0 ]) 0 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Incomplete Types
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 193
nodes.content: Incomplete Types are structures, unions or arrays whose members are not yet specified. In C, they are specified by forward declarations, which are defined later:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 194
nodes.content: struct cell ; /* forward declaration */ struct cell { char * name ; struct cell * next ; };
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 195
nodes.content: The straightforward translation into ctypes code would be this, but it does not work:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 196
nodes.content: >>> class cell ( Structure ): ... _fields_ = [( "name" , c_char_p ), ... ( "next" , POINTER ( cell ))] ... Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>" , line 1 , in <module> File "<stdin>" , line 2 , in cell NameError : name 'cell' is not defined >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 197
nodes.content: because the new class cell is not available in the class statement itself. In ctypes , we can define the cell class and set the _fields_ attribute later, after the class statement:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 198
nodes.content: >>> from ctypes import * >>> class cell ( Structure ): ... pass ... >>> cell . _fields_ = [( "name" , c_char_p ), ... ( "next" , POINTER ( cell ))] >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 199
nodes.content: Let’s try it. We create two instances of cell , and let them point to each other, and finally follow the pointer chain a few times:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 200
nodes.content: >>> c1 = cell () >>> c1 . name = b "foo" >>> c2 = cell () >>> c2 . name = b "bar" >>> c1 . next = pointer ( c2 ) >>> c2 . next = pointer ( c1 ) >>> p = c1 >>> for i in range ( 8 ): ... print ( p . name , end = " " ) ... p = p . next [ 0 ] ... foo bar foo bar foo bar foo bar >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Callback functions
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 202
nodes.content: ctypes allows creating C callable function pointers from Python callables. These are sometimes called callback functions .
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 203
nodes.content: First, you must create a class for the callback function. The class knows the calling convention, the return type, and the number and types of arguments this function will receive.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 204
nodes.content: The CFUNCTYPE() factory function creates types for callback functions using the cdecl calling convention. On Windows, the WINFUNCTYPE() factory function creates types for callback functions using the stdcall calling convention.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 205
nodes.content: Both of these factory functions are called with the result type as first argument, and the callback functions expected argument types as the remaining arguments.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 206
nodes.content: I will present an example here which uses the standard C library’s qsort() function, that is used to sort items with the help of a callback function. qsort() will be used to sort an array of integers:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 207
nodes.content: >>> IntArray5 = c_int * 5 >>> ia = IntArray5 ( 5 , 1 , 7 , 33 , 99 ) >>> qsort = libc . qsort >>> qsort . restype = None >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 208
nodes.content: qsort() must be called with a pointer to the data to sort, the number of items in the data array, the size of one item, and a pointer to the comparison function, the callback. The callback will then be called with two pointers to items, and it must return a negative integer if the first item is smaller than the second, a zero if they are equal, and a positive integer otherwise.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 209
nodes.content: So our callback function receives pointers to integers, and must return an integer. First we create the type for the callback function:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 210
nodes.content: >>> CMPFUNC = CFUNCTYPE ( c_int , POINTER ( c_int ), POINTER ( c_int )) >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 211
nodes.content: To get started, here is a simple callback that shows the values it gets passed:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 212
nodes.content: >>> def py_cmp_func ( a , b ): ... print ( "py_cmp_func" , a [ 0 ], b [ 0 ]) ... return 0 ... >>> cmp_func = CMPFUNC ( py_cmp_func ) >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 213
nodes.content: The result:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 214
nodes.content: >>> qsort ( ia , len ( ia ), sizeof ( c_int ), cmp_func ) py_cmp_func 5 1 py_cmp_func 33 99 py_cmp_func 7 33 py_cmp_func 5 7 py_cmp_func 1 7 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 215
nodes.content: Now we can actually compare the two items and return a useful result:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 216
nodes.content: >>> def py_cmp_func ( a , b ): ... print ( "py_cmp_func" , a [ 0 ], b [ 0 ]) ... return a [ 0 ] - b [ 0 ] ... >>> >>> qsort ( ia , len ( ia ), sizeof ( c_int ), CMPFUNC ( py_cmp_func )) py_cmp_func 5 1 py_cmp_func 33 99 py_cmp_func 7 33 py_cmp_func 1 7 py_cmp_func 5 7 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 217
nodes.content: As we can easily check, our array is sorted now:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 218
nodes.content: >>> for i in ia : print ( i , end = " " ) ... 1 5 7 33 99 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 219
nodes.content: The function factories can be used as decorator factories, so we may as well write:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 220
nodes.content: >>> @CFUNCTYPE ( c_int , POINTER ( c_int ), POINTER ( c_int )) ... def py_cmp_func ( a , b ): ... print ( "py_cmp_func" , a [ 0 ], b [ 0 ]) ... return a [ 0 ] - b [ 0 ] ... >>> qsort ( ia , len ( ia ), sizeof ( c_int ), py_cmp_func ) py_cmp_func 5 1 py_cmp_func 33 99 py_cmp_func 7 33 py_cmp_func 1 7 py_cmp_func 5 7 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 221
nodes.content: Note
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 222
nodes.content: Make sure you keep references to CFUNCTYPE() objects as long as they are used from C code. ctypes doesn’t, and if you don’t, they may be garbage collected, crashing your program when a callback is made.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 223
nodes.content: Also, note that if the callback function is called in a thread created outside of Python’s control (e.g. by the foreign code that calls the callback), ctypes creates a new dummy Python thread on every invocation. This behavior is correct for most purposes, but it means that values stored with threading.local will not survive across different callbacks, even when those calls are made from the same C thread.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Accessing values exported from dlls
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 225
nodes.content: Some shared libraries not only export functions, they also export variables. An example in the Python library itself is the Py_Version , Python runtime version number encoded in a single constant integer.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 226
nodes.content: ctypes can access values like this with the in_dll() class methods of the type. pythonapi is a predefined symbol giving access to the Python C api:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 227
nodes.content: >>> version = ctypes . c_int . in_dll ( ctypes . pythonapi , "Py_Version" ) >>> print ( hex ( version . value )) 0x30c00a0
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 228
nodes.content: An extended example which also demonstrates the use of pointers accesses the PyImport_FrozenModules pointer exported by Python.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 229
nodes.content: Quoting the docs for that value:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 230
nodes.content: This pointer is initialized to point to an array of _frozen records, terminated by one whose members are all NULL or zero. When a frozen module is imported, it is searched in this table. Third-party code could play tricks with this to provide a dynamically created collection of frozen modules.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 231
nodes.content: So manipulating this pointer could even prove useful. To restrict the example size, we show only how this table can be read with ctypes :
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 232
nodes.content: >>> from ctypes import * >>> >>> class struct_frozen ( Structure ): ... _fields_ = [( "name" , c_char_p ), ... ( "code" , POINTER ( c_ubyte )), ... ( "size" , c_int ), ... ( "get_code" , POINTER ( c_ubyte )), # Function pointer ... ] ... >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 233
nodes.content: We have defined the _frozen data type, so we can get the pointer to the table:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 234
nodes.content: >>> FrozenTable = POINTER ( struct_frozen ) >>> table = FrozenTable . in_dll ( pythonapi , "_PyImport_FrozenBootstrap" ) >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 235
nodes.content: Since table is a pointer to the array of struct_frozen records, we can iterate over it, but we just have to make sure that our loop terminates, because pointers have no size. Sooner or later it would probably crash with an access violation or whatever, so it’s better to break out of the loop when we hit the NULL entry:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 236
nodes.content: >>> for item in table : ... if item . name is None : ... break ... print ( item . name . decode ( "ascii" ), item . size ) ... _frozen_importlib 31764 _frozen_importlib_external 41499 zipimport 12345 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 237
nodes.content: The fact that standard Python has a frozen module and a frozen package (indicated by the negative size member) is not well known, it is only used for testing. Try it out with import __hello__ for example.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Surprises
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 239
nodes.content: There are some edges in ctypes where you might expect something other than what actually happens.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 240
nodes.content: Consider the following example:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 241
nodes.content: >>> from ctypes import * >>> class POINT ( Structure ): ... _fields_ = ( "x" , c_int ), ( "y" , c_int ) ... >>> class RECT ( Structure ): ... _fields_ = ( "a" , POINT ), ( "b" , POINT ) ... >>> p1 = POINT ( 1 , 2 ) >>> p2 = POINT ( 3 , 4 ) >>> rc = RECT ( p1 , p2 ) >>> print ( rc . a . x , rc . a . y , rc . b . x , rc . b . y ) 1 2 3 4 >>> # now swap the two points >>> rc . a , rc . b = rc . b , rc . a >>> print ( rc . a . x , rc . a . y , rc . b . x , rc . b . y ) 3 4 3 4 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 242
nodes.content: Hm. We certainly expected the last statement to print 3 4 1 2 . What happened? Here are the steps of the rc.a, rc.b = rc.b, rc.a line above:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 243
nodes.content: >>> temp0 , temp1 = rc . b , rc . a >>> rc . a = temp0 >>> rc . b = temp1 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 244
nodes.content: Note that temp0 and temp1 are objects still using the internal buffer of the rc object above. So executing rc.a = temp0 copies the buffer contents of temp0 into rc ‘s buffer. This, in turn, changes the contents of temp1 . So, the last assignment rc.b = temp1 , doesn’t have the expected effect.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 245
nodes.content: Keep in mind that retrieving sub-objects from Structure, Unions, and Arrays doesn’t copy the sub-object, instead it retrieves a wrapper object accessing the root-object’s underlying buffer.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 246
nodes.content: Another example that may behave differently from what one would expect is this:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 247
nodes.content: >>> s = c_char_p () >>> s . value = b "abc def ghi" >>> s . value b'abc def ghi' >>> s . value is s . value False >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 248
nodes.content: Note
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 249
nodes.content: Objects instantiated from c_char_p can only have their value set to bytes or integers.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 250
nodes.content: Why is it printing False ? ctypes instances are objects containing a memory block plus some descriptor s accessing the contents of the memory. Storing a Python object in the memory block does not store the object itself, instead the contents of the object is stored. Accessing the contents again constructs a new Python object each time!
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Variable-sized data types
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 252
nodes.content: ctypes provides some support for variable-sized arrays and structures.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 253
nodes.content: The resize() function can be used to resize the memory buffer of an existing ctypes object. The function takes the object as first argument, and the requested size in bytes as the second argument. The memory block cannot be made smaller than the natural memory block specified by the objects type, a ValueError is raised if this is tried:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 254
nodes.content: >>> short_array = ( c_short * 4 )() >>> print ( sizeof ( short_array )) 8 >>> resize ( short_array , 4 ) Traceback (most recent call last): ... ValueError : minimum size is 8 >>> resize ( short_array , 32 ) >>> sizeof ( short_array ) 32 >>> sizeof ( type ( short_array )) 8 >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 255
nodes.content: This is nice and fine, but how would one access the additional elements contained in this array? Since the type still only knows about 4 elements, we get errors accessing other elements:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 256
nodes.content: >>> short_array [:] [0, 0, 0, 0] >>> short_array [ 7 ] Traceback (most recent call last): ... IndexError : invalid index >>>
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 257
nodes.content: Another way to use variable-sized data types with ctypes is to use the dynamic nature of Python, and (re-)define the data type after the required size is already known, on a case by case basis.

nodes.title: Finding shared libraries
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 260
nodes.content: When programming in a compiled language, shared libraries are accessed when compiling/linking a program, and when the program is run.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 261
nodes.content: The purpose of the find_library() function is to locate a library in a way similar to what the compiler or runtime loader does (on platforms with several versions of a shared library the most recent should be loaded), while the ctypes library loaders act like when a program is run, and call the runtime loader directly.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 262
nodes.content: The ctypes.util module provides a function which can help to determine the library to load.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: ctypes.util. find_library ( name )
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 264
nodes.content: ctypes.util. find_library ( name )
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 265
nodes.content: Try to find a library and return a pathname. name is the library name without any prefix like lib , suffix like .so , .dylib or version number (this is the form used for the posix linker option -l ). If no library can be found, returns None .
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 266
nodes.content: The exact functionality is system dependent.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 267
nodes.content: On Linux, find_library() tries to run external programs ( /sbin/ldconfig , gcc , objdump and ld ) to find the library file. It returns the filename of the library file.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 268
nodes.content: Note that if the output of these programs does not correspond to the dynamic linker used by Python, the result of this function may be misleading.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 269
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.6: On Linux, the value of the environment variable LD_LIBRARY_PATH is used when searching for libraries, if a library cannot be found by any other means.
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python

nodes.title: Passage 270
nodes.content: Here are some examples:
path: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python
