nodes.title: Passage 21
nodes.content: A type alias is defined using the type statement, which creates an instance of TypeAliasType . In this example, Vector and list[float] will be treated equivalently by static type checkers:

nodes.title: Passage 22
nodes.content: type Vector = list [ float ] def scale ( scalar : float , vector : Vector ) -> Vector : return [ scalar * num for num in vector ] # passes type checking; a list of floats qualifies as a Vector. new_vector = scale ( 2.0 , [ 1.0 , - 4.2 , 5.4 ])

nodes.title: Passage 23
nodes.content: Type aliases are useful for simplifying complex type signatures. For example:

nodes.title: Passage 24
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Sequence type ConnectionOptions = dict [ str , str ] type Address = tuple [ str , int ] type Server = tuple [ Address , ConnectionOptions ] def broadcast_message ( message : str , servers : Sequence [ Server ]) -> None : ... # The static type checker will treat the previous type signature as # being exactly equivalent to this one. def broadcast_message ( message : str , servers : Sequence [ tuple [ tuple [ str , int ], dict [ str , str ]]] ) -> None : ...

nodes.title: Passage 25
nodes.content: The type statement is new in Python 3.12. For backwards compatibility, type aliases can also be created through simple assignment:

nodes.title: Passage 26
nodes.content: Vector = list [ float ]

nodes.title: Passage 27
nodes.content: Or marked with TypeAlias to make it explicit that this is a type alias, not a normal variable assignment:

nodes.title: Passage 28
nodes.content: from typing import TypeAlias Vector : TypeAlias = list [ float ]

nodes.title: Passage 30
nodes.content: Use the NewType helper to create distinct types:

nodes.title: Passage 31
nodes.content: from typing import NewType UserId = NewType ( 'UserId' , int ) some_id = UserId ( 524313 )

nodes.title: Passage 32
nodes.content: The static type checker will treat the new type as if it were a subclass of the original type. This is useful in helping catch logical errors:

nodes.title: Passage 33
nodes.content: def get_user_name ( user_id : UserId ) -> str : ... # passes type checking user_a = get_user_name ( UserId ( 42351 )) # fails type checking; an int is not a UserId user_b = get_user_name ( - 1 )

nodes.title: Passage 34
nodes.content: You may still perform all int operations on a variable of type UserId , but the result will always be of type int . This lets you pass in a UserId wherever an int might be expected, but will prevent you from accidentally creating a UserId in an invalid way:

nodes.title: Passage 35
nodes.content: # 'output' is of type 'int', not 'UserId' output = UserId ( 23413 ) + UserId ( 54341 )

nodes.title: Passage 36
nodes.content: Note that these checks are enforced only by the static type checker. At runtime, the statement Derived = NewType('Derived', Base) will make Derived a callable that immediately returns whatever parameter you pass it. That means the expression Derived(some_value) does not create a new class or introduce much overhead beyond that of a regular function call.

nodes.title: Passage 37
nodes.content: More precisely, the expression some_value is Derived(some_value) is always true at runtime.

nodes.title: Passage 38
nodes.content: It is invalid to create a subtype of Derived :

nodes.title: Passage 39
nodes.content: from typing import NewType UserId = NewType ( 'UserId' , int ) # Fails at runtime and does not pass type checking class AdminUserId ( UserId ): pass

nodes.title: Passage 40
nodes.content: However, it is possible to create a NewType based on a ‘derived’ NewType :

nodes.title: Passage 41
nodes.content: from typing import NewType UserId = NewType ( 'UserId' , int ) ProUserId = NewType ( 'ProUserId' , UserId )

nodes.title: Passage 42
nodes.content: and typechecking for ProUserId will work as expected.

nodes.title: Passage 43
nodes.content: See PEP 484 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 44
nodes.content: Note

nodes.title: Passage 45
nodes.content: Recall that the use of a type alias declares two types to be equivalent to one another. Doing type Alias = Original will make the static type checker treat Alias as being exactly equivalent to Original in all cases. This is useful when you want to simplify complex type signatures.

nodes.title: Passage 46
nodes.content: In contrast, NewType declares one type to be a subtype of another. Doing Derived = NewType('Derived', Original) will make the static type checker treat Derived as a subclass of Original , which means a value of type Original cannot be used in places where a value of type Derived is expected. This is useful when you want to prevent logic errors with minimal runtime cost.

nodes.title: Passage 47
nodes.content: Added in version 3.5.2.

nodes.title: Passage 48
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.10: NewType is now a class rather than a function. As a result, there is some additional runtime cost when calling NewType over a regular function.

nodes.title: Passage 49
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.11: The performance of calling NewType has been restored to its level in Python 3.9.

nodes.title: Passage 51
nodes.content: Functions – or other callable objects – can be annotated using collections.abc.Callable or deprecated typing.Callable . Callable[[int], str] signifies a function that takes a single parameter of type int and returns a str .

nodes.title: Passage 52
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 53
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Callable , Awaitable def feeder ( get_next_item : Callable [[], str ]) -> None : ... # Body def async_query ( on_success : Callable [[ int ], None ], on_error : Callable [[ int , Exception ], None ]) -> None : ... # Body async def on_update ( value : str ) -> None : ... # Body callback : Callable [[ str ], Awaitable [ None ]] = on_update

nodes.title: Passage 54
nodes.content: The subscription syntax must always be used with exactly two values: the argument list and the return type. The argument list must be a list of types, a ParamSpec , Concatenate , or an ellipsis ( ... ). The return type must be a single type.

nodes.title: Passage 55
nodes.content: If a literal ellipsis ... is given as the argument list, it indicates that a callable with any arbitrary parameter list would be acceptable:

nodes.title: Passage 56
nodes.content: def concat ( x : str , y : str ) -> str : return x + y x : Callable [ ... , str ] x = str # OK x = concat # Also OK

nodes.title: Passage 57
nodes.content: Callable cannot express complex signatures such as functions that take a variadic number of arguments, overloaded functions , or functions that have keyword-only parameters. However, these signatures can be expressed by defining a Protocol class with a __call__() method:

nodes.title: Passage 58
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Iterable from typing import Protocol class Combiner ( Protocol ): def __call__ ( self , * vals : bytes , maxlen : int | None = None ) -> list [ bytes ]: ... def batch_proc ( data : Iterable [ bytes ], cb_results : Combiner ) -> bytes : for item in data : ... def good_cb ( * vals : bytes , maxlen : int | None = None ) -> list [ bytes ]: ... def bad_cb ( * vals : bytes , maxitems : int | None ) -> list [ bytes ]: ... batch_proc ([], good_cb ) # OK batch_proc ([], bad_cb ) # Error! Argument 2 has incompatible type because of # different name and kind in the callback

nodes.title: Passage 59
nodes.content: Callables which take other callables as arguments may indicate that their parameter types are dependent on each other using ParamSpec . Additionally, if that callable adds or removes arguments from other callables, the Concatenate operator may be used. They take the form Callable[ParamSpecVariable, ReturnType] and Callable[Concatenate[Arg1Type, Arg2Type, ..., ParamSpecVariable], ReturnType] respectively.

nodes.title: Passage 60
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.10: Callable now supports ParamSpec and Concatenate . See PEP 612 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 61
nodes.content: See also

nodes.title: Passage 62
nodes.content: The documentation for ParamSpec and Concatenate provides examples of usage in Callable .

nodes.title: Passage 64
nodes.content: Since type information about objects kept in containers cannot be statically inferred in a generic way, many container classes in the standard library support subscription to denote the expected types of container elements.

nodes.title: Passage 65
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Mapping , Sequence class Employee : ... # Sequence[Employee] indicates that all elements in the sequence # must be instances of "Employee". # Mapping[str, str] indicates that all keys and all values in the mapping # must be strings. def notify_by_email ( employees : Sequence [ Employee ], overrides : Mapping [ str , str ]) -> None : ...

nodes.title: Passage 66
nodes.content: Generic functions and classes can be parameterized by using type parameter syntax :

nodes.title: Passage 67
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Sequence def first [ T ]( l : Sequence [ T ]) -> T : # Function is generic over the TypeVar "T" return l [ 0 ]

nodes.title: Passage 68
nodes.content: Or by using the TypeVar factory directly:

nodes.title: Passage 69
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Sequence from typing import TypeVar U = TypeVar ( 'U' ) # Declare type variable "U" def second ( l : Sequence [ U ]) -> U : # Function is generic over the TypeVar "U" return l [ 1 ]

nodes.title: Passage 70
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.12: Syntactic support for generics is new in Python 3.12.

nodes.title: Passage 72
nodes.content: For most containers in Python, the typing system assumes that all elements in the container will be of the same type. For example:

nodes.title: Passage 73
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Mapping # Type checker will infer that all elements in ``x`` are meant to be ints x : list [ int ] = [] # Type checker error: ``list`` only accepts a single type argument: y : list [ int , str ] = [ 1 , 'foo' ] # Type checker will infer that all keys in ``z`` are meant to be strings, # and that all values in ``z`` are meant to be either strings or ints z : Mapping [ str , str | int ] = {}

nodes.title: Passage 74
nodes.content: list only accepts one type argument, so a type checker would emit an error on the y assignment above. Similarly, Mapping only accepts two type arguments: the first indicates the type of the keys, and the second indicates the type of the values.

nodes.title: Passage 75
nodes.content: Unlike most other Python containers, however, it is common in idiomatic Python code for tuples to have elements which are not all of the same type. For this reason, tuples are special-cased in Python’s typing system. tuple accepts any number of type arguments:

nodes.title: Passage 76
nodes.content: # OK: ``x`` is assigned to a tuple of length 1 where the sole element is an int x : tuple [ int ] = ( 5 ,) # OK: ``y`` is assigned to a tuple of length 2; # element 1 is an int, element 2 is a str y : tuple [ int , str ] = ( 5 , "foo" ) # Error: the type annotation indicates a tuple of length 1, # but ``z`` has been assigned to a tuple of length 3 z : tuple [ int ] = ( 1 , 2 , 3 )

nodes.title: Passage 77
nodes.content: To denote a tuple which could be of any length, and in which all elements are of the same type T , use the literal ellipsis ... : tuple[T, ...] . To denote an empty tuple, use tuple[()] . Using plain tuple as an annotation is equivalent to using tuple[Any, ...] :

nodes.title: Passage 78
nodes.content: x : tuple [ int , ... ] = ( 1 , 2 ) # These reassignments are OK: ``tuple[int, ...]`` indicates x can be of any length x = ( 1 , 2 , 3 ) x = () # This reassignment is an error: all elements in ``x`` must be ints x = ( "foo" , "bar" ) # ``y`` can only ever be assigned to an empty tuple y : tuple [()] = () z : tuple = ( "foo" , "bar" ) # These reassignments are OK: plain ``tuple`` is equivalent to ``tuple[Any, ...]`` z = ( 1 , 2 , 3 ) z = ()

nodes.title: Passage 80
nodes.content: A variable annotated with C may accept a value of type C . In contrast, a variable annotated with type[C] (or deprecated typing.Type[C] ) may accept values that are classes themselves – specifically, it will accept the class object of C . For example:

nodes.title: Passage 81
nodes.content: a = 3 # Has type ``int`` b = int # Has type ``type[int]`` c = type ( a ) # Also has type ``type[int]``

nodes.title: Passage 82
nodes.content: Note that type[C] is covariant:

nodes.title: Passage 83
nodes.content: class User : ... class ProUser ( User ): ... class TeamUser ( User ): ... def make_new_user ( user_class : type [ User ]) -> User : # ... return user_class () make_new_user ( User ) # OK make_new_user ( ProUser ) # Also OK: ``type[ProUser]`` is a subtype of ``type[User]`` make_new_user ( TeamUser ) # Still fine make_new_user ( User ()) # Error: expected ``type[User]`` but got ``User`` make_new_user ( int ) # Error: ``type[int]`` is not a subtype of ``type[User]``

nodes.title: Passage 84
nodes.content: The only legal parameters for type are classes, Any , type variables , and unions of any of these types. For example:

nodes.title: Passage 85
nodes.content: def new_non_team_user ( user_class : type [ BasicUser | ProUser ]): ... new_non_team_user ( BasicUser ) # OK new_non_team_user ( ProUser ) # OK new_non_team_user ( TeamUser ) # Error: ``type[TeamUser]`` is not a subtype # of ``type[BasicUser | ProUser]`` new_non_team_user ( User ) # Also an error

nodes.title: Passage 86
nodes.content: type[Any] is equivalent to type , which is the root of Python’s metaclass hierarchy .

nodes.title: Passage 88
nodes.content: A generator can be annotated using the generic type Generator[YieldType, SendType, ReturnType] . For example:

nodes.title: Passage 89
nodes.content: def echo_round () -> Generator [ int , float , str ]: sent = yield 0 while sent >= 0 : sent = yield round ( sent ) return 'Done'

nodes.title: Passage 90
nodes.content: Note that unlike many other generic classes in the standard library, the SendType of Generator behaves contravariantly, not covariantly or invariantly.

nodes.title: Passage 91
nodes.content: The SendType and ReturnType parameters default to None :

nodes.title: Passage 92
nodes.content: def infinite_stream ( start : int ) -> Generator [ int ]: while True : yield start start += 1

nodes.title: Passage 93
nodes.content: It is also possible to set these types explicitly:

nodes.title: Passage 94
nodes.content: def infinite_stream ( start : int ) -> Generator [ int , None , None ]: while True : yield start start += 1

nodes.title: Passage 95
nodes.content: Simple generators that only ever yield values can also be annotated as having a return type of either Iterable[YieldType] or Iterator[YieldType] :

nodes.title: Passage 96
nodes.content: def infinite_stream ( start : int ) -> Iterator [ int ]: while True : yield start start += 1

nodes.title: Passage 97
nodes.content: Async generators are handled in a similar fashion, but don’t expect a ReturnType type argument ( AsyncGenerator[YieldType, SendType] ). The SendType argument defaults to None , so the following definitions are equivalent:

nodes.title: Passage 98
nodes.content: async def infinite_stream ( start : int ) -> AsyncGenerator [ int ]: while True : yield start start = await increment ( start ) async def infinite_stream ( start : int ) -> AsyncGenerator [ int , None ]: while True : yield start start = await increment ( start )

nodes.title: Passage 99
nodes.content: As in the synchronous case, AsyncIterable[YieldType] and AsyncIterator[YieldType] are available as well:

nodes.title: Passage 100
nodes.content: async def infinite_stream ( start : int ) -> AsyncIterator [ int ]: while True : yield start start = await increment ( start )

nodes.title: Passage 101
nodes.content: Coroutines can be annotated using Coroutine[YieldType, SendType, ReturnType] . Generic arguments correspond to those of Generator , for example:

nodes.title: Passage 102
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Coroutine c : Coroutine [ list [ str ], str , int ] # Some coroutine defined elsewhere x = c . send ( 'hi' ) # Inferred type of 'x' is list[str] async def bar () -> None : y = await c # Inferred type of 'y' is int

nodes.title: Passage 104
nodes.content: A user-defined class can be defined as a generic class.

nodes.title: Passage 105
nodes.content: from logging import Logger class LoggedVar [ T ]: def __init__ ( self , value : T , name : str , logger : Logger ) -> None : self . name = name self . logger = logger self . value = value def set ( self , new : T ) -> None : self . log ( 'Set ' + repr ( self . value )) self . value = new def get ( self ) -> T : self . log ( 'Get ' + repr ( self . value )) return self . value def log ( self , message : str ) -> None : self . logger . info ( ' %s : %s ' , self . name , message )

nodes.title: Passage 106
nodes.content: This syntax indicates that the class LoggedVar is parameterised around a single type variable T . This also makes T valid as a type within the class body.

nodes.title: Passage 107
nodes.content: Generic classes implicitly inherit from Generic . For compatibility with Python 3.11 and lower, it is also possible to inherit explicitly from Generic to indicate a generic class:

nodes.title: Passage 108
nodes.content: from typing import TypeVar , Generic T = TypeVar ( 'T' ) class LoggedVar ( Generic [ T ]): ...

nodes.title: Passage 109
nodes.content: Generic classes have __class_getitem__() methods, meaning they can be parameterised at runtime (e.g. LoggedVar[int] below):

nodes.title: Passage 110
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Iterable def zero_all_vars ( vars : Iterable [ LoggedVar [ int ]]) -> None : for var in vars : var . set ( 0 )

nodes.title: Passage 111
nodes.content: A generic type can have any number of type variables. All varieties of TypeVar are permissible as parameters for a generic type:

nodes.title: Passage 112
nodes.content: from typing import TypeVar , Generic , Sequence class WeirdTrio [ T , B : Sequence [ bytes ], S : ( int , str )]: ... OldT = TypeVar ( 'OldT' , contravariant = True ) OldB = TypeVar ( 'OldB' , bound = Sequence [ bytes ], covariant = True ) OldS = TypeVar ( 'OldS' , int , str ) class OldWeirdTrio ( Generic [ OldT , OldB , OldS ]): ...

nodes.title: Passage 113
nodes.content: Each type variable argument to Generic must be distinct. This is thus invalid:

nodes.title: Passage 114
nodes.content: from typing import TypeVar , Generic ... class Pair [ M , M ]: # SyntaxError ... T = TypeVar ( 'T' ) class Pair ( Generic [ T , T ]): # INVALID ...

nodes.title: Passage 115
nodes.content: Generic classes can also inherit from other classes:

nodes.title: Passage 116
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Sized class LinkedList [ T ]( Sized ): ...

nodes.title: Passage 117
nodes.content: When inheriting from generic classes, some type parameters could be fixed:

nodes.title: Passage 118
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Mapping class MyDict [ T ]( Mapping [ str , T ]): ...

nodes.title: Passage 119
nodes.content: In this case MyDict has a single parameter, T .

nodes.title: Passage 120
nodes.content: Using a generic class without specifying type parameters assumes Any for each position. In the following example, MyIterable is not generic but implicitly inherits from Iterable[Any] :

nodes.title: Passage 121
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Iterable class MyIterable ( Iterable ): # Same as Iterable[Any] ...

nodes.title: Passage 122
nodes.content: User-defined generic type aliases are also supported. Examples:

nodes.title: Passage 123
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Iterable type Response [ S ] = Iterable [ S ] | int # Return type here is same as Iterable[str] | int def response ( query : str ) -> Response [ str ]: ... type Vec [ T ] = Iterable [ tuple [ T , T ]] def inproduct [ T : ( int , float , complex )]( v : Vec [ T ]) -> T : # Same as Iterable[tuple[T, T]] return sum ( x * y for x , y in v )

nodes.title: Passage 124
nodes.content: For backward compatibility, generic type aliases can also be created through a simple assignment:

nodes.title: Passage 125
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Iterable from typing import TypeVar S = TypeVar ( "S" ) Response = Iterable [ S ] | int

nodes.title: Passage 126
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.7: Generic no longer has a custom metaclass.

nodes.title: Passage 127
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.12: Syntactic support for generics and type aliases is new in version 3.12. Previously, generic classes had to explicitly inherit from Generic or contain a type variable in one of their bases.

nodes.title: Passage 128
nodes.content: User-defined generics for parameter expressions are also supported via parameter specification variables in the form [**P] . The behavior is consistent with type variables’ described above as parameter specification variables are treated by the typing module as a specialized type variable. The one exception to this is that a list of types can be used to substitute a ParamSpec :

nodes.title: Passage 129
nodes.content: >>> class Z [ T , ** P ]: ... # T is a TypeVar; P is a ParamSpec ... >>> Z [ int , [ dict , float ]] __main__.Z[int, [dict, float]]

nodes.title: Passage 130
nodes.content: Classes generic over a ParamSpec can also be created using explicit inheritance from Generic . In this case, ** is not used:

nodes.title: Passage 131
nodes.content: from typing import ParamSpec , Generic P = ParamSpec ( 'P' ) class Z ( Generic [ P ]): ...

nodes.title: Passage 132
nodes.content: Another difference between TypeVar and ParamSpec is that a generic with only one parameter specification variable will accept parameter lists in the forms X[[Type1, Type2, ...]] and also X[Type1, Type2, ...] for aesthetic reasons. Internally, the latter is converted to the former, so the following are equivalent:

nodes.title: Passage 133
nodes.content: >>> class X [ ** P ]: ... ... >>> X [ int , str ] __main__.X[[int, str]] >>> X [[ int , str ]] __main__.X[[int, str]]

nodes.title: Passage 134
nodes.content: Note that generics with ParamSpec may not have correct __parameters__ after substitution in some cases because they are intended primarily for static type checking.

nodes.title: Passage 135
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.10: Generic can now be parameterized over parameter expressions. See ParamSpec and PEP 612 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 136
nodes.content: A user-defined generic class can have ABCs as base classes without a metaclass conflict. Generic metaclasses are not supported. The outcome of parameterizing generics is cached, and most types in the typing module are hashable and comparable for equality.

nodes.title: Passage 138
nodes.content: A special kind of type is Any . A static type checker will treat every type as assignable to Any and Any as assignable to every type.

nodes.title: Passage 139
nodes.content: This means that it is possible to perform any operation or method call on a value of type Any and assign it to any variable:

nodes.title: Passage 140
nodes.content: from typing import Any a : Any = None a = [] # OK a = 2 # OK s : str = '' s = a # OK def foo ( item : Any ) -> int : # Passes type checking; 'item' could be any type, # and that type might have a 'bar' method item . bar () ...

nodes.title: Passage 141
nodes.content: Notice that no type checking is performed when assigning a value of type Any to a more precise type. For example, the static type checker did not report an error when assigning a to s even though s was declared to be of type str and receives an int value at runtime!

nodes.title: Passage 142
nodes.content: Furthermore, all functions without a return type or parameter types will implicitly default to using Any :

nodes.title: Passage 143
nodes.content: def legacy_parser ( text ): ... return data # A static type checker will treat the above # as having the same signature as: def legacy_parser ( text : Any ) -> Any : ... return data

nodes.title: Passage 144
nodes.content: This behavior allows Any to be used as an escape hatch when you need to mix dynamically and statically typed code.

nodes.title: Passage 145
nodes.content: Contrast the behavior of Any with the behavior of object . Similar to Any , every type is a subtype of object . However, unlike Any , the reverse is not true: object is not a subtype of every other type.

nodes.title: Passage 146
nodes.content: That means when the type of a value is object , a type checker will reject almost all operations on it, and assigning it to a variable (or using it as a return value) of a more specialized type is a type error. For example:

nodes.title: Passage 147
nodes.content: def hash_a ( item : object ) -> int : # Fails type checking; an object does not have a 'magic' method. item . magic () ... def hash_b ( item : Any ) -> int : # Passes type checking item . magic () ... # Passes type checking, since ints and strs are subclasses of object hash_a ( 42 ) hash_a ( "foo" ) # Passes type checking, since Any is assignable to all types hash_b ( 42 ) hash_b ( "foo" )

nodes.title: Passage 148
nodes.content: Use object to indicate that a value could be any type in a typesafe manner. Use Any to indicate that a value is dynamically typed.

nodes.title: Passage 150
nodes.content: Initially PEP 484 defined the Python static type system as using nominal subtyping . This means that a class A is allowed where a class B is expected if and only if A is a subclass of B .

nodes.title: Passage 151
nodes.content: This requirement previously also applied to abstract base classes, such as Iterable . The problem with this approach is that a class had to be explicitly marked to support them, which is unpythonic and unlike what one would normally do in idiomatic dynamically typed Python code. For example, this conforms to PEP 484 :

nodes.title: Passage 152
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Sized , Iterable , Iterator class Bucket ( Sized , Iterable [ int ]): ... def __len__ ( self ) -> int : ... def __iter__ ( self ) -> Iterator [ int ]: ...

nodes.title: Passage 153
nodes.content: PEP 544 solves this problem by allowing users to write the above code without explicit base classes in the class definition, allowing Bucket to be implicitly considered a subtype of both Sized and Iterable[int] by static type checkers. This is known as structural subtyping (or static duck-typing):

nodes.title: Passage 154
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Iterator , Iterable class Bucket : # Note: no base classes ... def __len__ ( self ) -> int : ... def __iter__ ( self ) -> Iterator [ int ]: ... def collect ( items : Iterable [ int ]) -> int : ... result = collect ( Bucket ()) # Passes type check

nodes.title: Passage 155
nodes.content: Moreover, by subclassing a special class Protocol , a user can define new custom protocols to fully enjoy structural subtyping (see examples below).

nodes.title: Passage 157
nodes.content: The typing module defines the following classes, functions and decorators.

nodes.title: Passage 160
nodes.content: These can be used as types in annotations. They do not support subscription using [] .

nodes.title: Passage 162
nodes.content: typing. Any

nodes.title: Passage 163
nodes.content: Special type indicating an unconstrained type.

nodes.title: Passage 164
nodes.content: Every type is assignable to Any .

nodes.title: Passage 165
nodes.content: Any is assignable to every type.

nodes.title: Passage 166
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.11: Any can now be used as a base class. This can be useful for avoiding type checker errors with classes that can duck type anywhere or are highly dynamic.

nodes.title: Passage 168
nodes.content: typing. AnyStr

nodes.title: Passage 169
nodes.content: A constrained type variable .

nodes.title: Passage 170
nodes.content: Definition:

nodes.title: Passage 171
nodes.content: AnyStr = TypeVar ( 'AnyStr' , str , bytes )

nodes.title: Passage 172
nodes.content: AnyStr is meant to be used for functions that may accept str or bytes arguments but cannot allow the two to mix.

nodes.title: Passage 173
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 174
nodes.content: def concat ( a : AnyStr , b : AnyStr ) -> AnyStr : return a + b concat ( "foo" , "bar" ) # OK, output has type 'str' concat ( b "foo" , b "bar" ) # OK, output has type 'bytes' concat ( "foo" , b "bar" ) # Error, cannot mix str and bytes

nodes.title: Passage 175
nodes.content: Note that, despite its name, AnyStr has nothing to do with the Any type, nor does it mean “any string”. In particular, AnyStr and str | bytes are different from each other and have different use cases:

nodes.title: Passage 176
nodes.content: # Invalid use of AnyStr: # The type variable is used only once in the function signature, # so cannot be "solved" by the type checker def greet_bad ( cond : bool ) -> AnyStr : return "hi there!" if cond else b "greetings!" # The better way of annotating this function: def greet_proper ( cond : bool ) -> str | bytes : return "hi there!" if cond else b "greetings!"

nodes.title: Passage 177
nodes.content: Deprecated since version 3.13, will be removed in version 3.18: Deprecated in favor of the new type parameter syntax . Use class A[T: (str, bytes)]: ... instead of importing AnyStr . See PEP 695 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 178
nodes.content: In Python 3.16, AnyStr will be removed from typing.__all__ , and deprecation warnings will be emitted at runtime when it is accessed or imported from typing . AnyStr will be removed from typing in Python 3.18.

nodes.title: Passage 180
nodes.content: typing. LiteralString

nodes.title: Passage 181
nodes.content: Special type that includes only literal strings.

nodes.title: Passage 182
nodes.content: Any string literal is compatible with LiteralString , as is another LiteralString . However, an object typed as just str is not. A string created by composing LiteralString -typed objects is also acceptable as a LiteralString .

nodes.title: Passage 183
nodes.content: Example:

nodes.title: Passage 184
nodes.content: def run_query ( sql : LiteralString ) -> None : ... def caller ( arbitrary_string : str , literal_string : LiteralString ) -> None : run_query ( "SELECT * FROM students" ) # OK run_query ( literal_string ) # OK run_query ( "SELECT * FROM " + literal_string ) # OK run_query ( arbitrary_string ) # type checker error run_query ( # type checker error f "SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = { arbitrary_string } " )

nodes.title: Passage 185
nodes.content: LiteralString is useful for sensitive APIs where arbitrary user-generated strings could generate problems. For example, the two cases above that generate type checker errors could be vulnerable to an SQL injection attack.

nodes.title: Passage 186
nodes.content: See PEP 675 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 187
nodes.content: Added in version 3.11.

nodes.title: Passage 189
nodes.content: typing. Never

nodes.title: Passage 190
nodes.content: typing. NoReturn

nodes.title: Passage 191
nodes.content: Never and NoReturn represent the bottom type , a type that has no members.

nodes.title: Passage 192
nodes.content: They can be used to indicate that a function never returns, such as sys.exit() :

nodes.title: Passage 193
nodes.content: from typing import Never # or NoReturn def stop () -> Never : raise RuntimeError ( 'no way' )

nodes.title: Passage 194
nodes.content: Or to define a function that should never be called, as there are no valid arguments, such as assert_never() :

nodes.title: Passage 195
nodes.content: from typing import Never # or NoReturn def never_call_me ( arg : Never ) -> None : pass def int_or_str ( arg : int | str ) -> None : never_call_me ( arg ) # type checker error match arg : case int (): print ( "It's an int" ) case str (): print ( "It's a str" ) case _ : never_call_me ( arg ) # OK, arg is of type Never (or NoReturn)

nodes.title: Passage 196
nodes.content: Never and NoReturn have the same meaning in the type system and static type checkers treat both equivalently.

nodes.title: Passage 197
nodes.content: Added in version 3.6.2: Added NoReturn .

nodes.title: Passage 198
nodes.content: Added in version 3.11: Added Never .

nodes.title: Passage 200
nodes.content: typing. Self

nodes.title: Passage 201
nodes.content: Special type to represent the current enclosed class.

nodes.title: Passage 202
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 203
nodes.content: from typing import Self , reveal_type class Foo : def return_self ( self ) -> Self : ... return self class SubclassOfFoo ( Foo ): pass reveal_type ( Foo () . return_self ()) # Revealed type is "Foo" reveal_type ( SubclassOfFoo () . return_self ()) # Revealed type is "SubclassOfFoo"

nodes.title: Passage 204
nodes.content: This annotation is semantically equivalent to the following, albeit in a more succinct fashion:

nodes.title: Passage 205
nodes.content: from typing import TypeVar Self = TypeVar ( "Self" , bound = "Foo" ) class Foo : def return_self ( self : Self ) -> Self : ... return self

nodes.title: Passage 206
nodes.content: In general, if something returns self , as in the above examples, you should use Self as the return annotation. If Foo.return_self was annotated as returning "Foo" , then the type checker would infer the object returned from SubclassOfFoo.return_self as being of type Foo rather than SubclassOfFoo .

nodes.title: Passage 207
nodes.content: Other common use cases include:

nodes.title: Passage 208
nodes.content: classmethod s that are used as alternative constructors and return instances of the cls parameter.

nodes.title: Passage 209
nodes.content: Annotating an __enter__() method which returns self.

nodes.title: Passage 210
nodes.content: You should not use Self as the return annotation if the method is not guaranteed to return an instance of a subclass when the class is subclassed:

nodes.title: Passage 211
nodes.content: class Eggs : # Self would be an incorrect return annotation here, # as the object returned is always an instance of Eggs, # even in subclasses def returns_eggs ( self ) -> "Eggs" : return Eggs ()

nodes.title: Passage 212
nodes.content: See PEP 673 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 213
nodes.content: Added in version 3.11.

nodes.title: Passage 215
nodes.content: typing. TypeAlias

nodes.title: Passage 216
nodes.content: Special annotation for explicitly declaring a type alias .

nodes.title: Passage 217
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 218
nodes.content: from typing import TypeAlias Factors : TypeAlias = list [ int ]

nodes.title: Passage 219
nodes.content: TypeAlias is particularly useful on older Python versions for annotating aliases that make use of forward references, as it can be hard for type checkers to distinguish these from normal variable assignments:

nodes.title: Passage 220
nodes.content: from typing import Generic , TypeAlias , TypeVar T = TypeVar ( "T" ) # "Box" does not exist yet, # so we have to use quotes for the forward reference on Python <3.12. # Using ``TypeAlias`` tells the type checker that this is a type alias declaration, # not a variable assignment to a string. BoxOfStrings : TypeAlias = "Box[str]" class Box ( Generic [ T ]): @classmethod def make_box_of_strings ( cls ) -> BoxOfStrings : ...

nodes.title: Passage 221
nodes.content: See PEP 613 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 222
nodes.content: Added in version 3.10.

nodes.title: Passage 223
nodes.content: Deprecated since version 3.12: TypeAlias is deprecated in favor of the type statement, which creates instances of TypeAliasType and which natively supports forward references. Note that while TypeAlias and TypeAliasType serve similar purposes and have similar names, they are distinct and the latter is not the type of the former. Removal of TypeAlias is not currently planned, but users are encouraged to migrate to type statements.

nodes.title: Passage 225
nodes.content: These can be used as types in annotations. They all support subscription using [] , but each has a unique syntax.

nodes.title: Passage 227
nodes.content: typing. Union

nodes.title: Passage 228
nodes.content: Union type; Union[X, Y] is equivalent to X | Y and means either X or Y.

nodes.title: Passage 229
nodes.content: To define a union, use e.g. Union[int, str] or the shorthand int | str . Using that shorthand is recommended. Details:

nodes.title: Passage 230
nodes.content: The arguments must be types and there must be at least one.

nodes.title: Passage 231
nodes.content: Unions of unions are flattened, e.g.:

nodes.title: Passage 232
nodes.content: Union [ Union [ int , str ], float ] == Union [ int , str , float ]

nodes.title: Passage 233
nodes.content: However, this does not apply to unions referenced through a type alias, to avoid forcing evaluation of the underlying TypeAliasType :

nodes.title: Passage 234
nodes.content: type A = Union [ int , str ] Union [ A , float ] != Union [ int , str , float ]

nodes.title: Passage 235
nodes.content: Unions of a single argument vanish, e.g.:

nodes.title: Passage 236
nodes.content: Union [ int ] == int # The constructor actually returns int

nodes.title: Passage 237
nodes.content: Redundant arguments are skipped, e.g.:

nodes.title: Passage 238
nodes.content: Union [ int , str , int ] == Union [ int , str ] == int | str

nodes.title: Passage 239
nodes.content: When comparing unions, the argument order is ignored, e.g.:

nodes.title: Passage 240
nodes.content: Union [ int , str ] == Union [ str , int ]

nodes.title: Passage 241
nodes.content: You cannot subclass or instantiate a Union .

nodes.title: Passage 242
nodes.content: You cannot write Union[X][Y] .

nodes.title: Passage 243
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.7: Don’t remove explicit subclasses from unions at runtime.

nodes.title: Passage 244
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.10: Unions can now be written as X | Y . See union type expressions .

nodes.title: Passage 246
nodes.content: typing. Optional

nodes.title: Passage 247
nodes.content: Optional[X] is equivalent to X | None (or Union[X, None] ).

nodes.title: Passage 248
nodes.content: Note that this is not the same concept as an optional argument, which is one that has a default. An optional argument with a default does not require the Optional qualifier on its type annotation just because it is optional. For example:

nodes.title: Passage 249
nodes.content: def foo ( arg : int = 0 ) -> None : ...

nodes.title: Passage 250
nodes.content: On the other hand, if an explicit value of None is allowed, the use of Optional is appropriate, whether the argument is optional or not. For example:

nodes.title: Passage 251
nodes.content: def foo ( arg : Optional [ int ] = None ) -> None : ...

nodes.title: Passage 252
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.10: Optional can now be written as X | None . See union type expressions .

nodes.title: Passage 254
nodes.content: typing. Concatenate

nodes.title: Passage 255
nodes.content: Special form for annotating higher-order functions.

nodes.title: Passage 256
nodes.content: Concatenate can be used in conjunction with Callable and ParamSpec to annotate a higher-order callable which adds, removes, or transforms parameters of another callable. Usage is in the form Concatenate[Arg1Type, Arg2Type, ..., ParamSpecVariable] . Concatenate is valid when used in Callable type hints and when instantiating user-defined generic classes with ParamSpec parameters. The last parameter to Concatenate must be a ParamSpec or ellipsis ( ... ).

nodes.title: Passage 257
nodes.content: For example, to annotate a decorator with_lock which provides a threading.Lock to the decorated function, Concatenate can be used to indicate that with_lock expects a callable which takes in a Lock as the first argument, and returns a callable with a different type signature. In this case, the ParamSpec indicates that the returned callable’s parameter types are dependent on the parameter types of the callable being passed in:

nodes.title: Passage 258
nodes.content: from collections.abc import Callable from threading import Lock from typing import Concatenate # Use this lock to ensure that only one thread is executing a function # at any time. my_lock = Lock () def with_lock [ ** P , R ]( f : Callable [ Concatenate [ Lock , P ], R ]) -> Callable [ P , R ]: '''A type-safe decorator which provides a lock.''' def inner ( * args : P . args , ** kwargs : P . kwargs ) -> R : # Provide the lock as the first argument. return f ( my_lock , * args , ** kwargs ) return inner @with_lock def sum_threadsafe ( lock : Lock , numbers : list [ float ]) -> float : '''Add a list of numbers together in a thread-safe manner.''' with lock : return sum ( numbers ) # We don't need to pass in the lock ourselves thanks to the decorator. sum_threadsafe ([

nodes.title: Passage 260
nodes.content: Added in version 3.10.

nodes.title: Passage 261
nodes.content: See also

nodes.title: Passage 262
nodes.content: PEP 612 – Parameter Specification Variables (the PEP which introduced ParamSpec and Concatenate )

nodes.title: Passage 263
nodes.content: ParamSpec

nodes.title: Passage 264
nodes.content: Annotating callable objects

nodes.title: Passage 266
nodes.content: typing. Literal

nodes.title: Passage 267
nodes.content: Special typing form to define “literal types”.

nodes.title: Passage 268
nodes.content: Literal can be used to indicate to type checkers that the annotated object has a value equivalent to one of the provided literals.

nodes.title: Passage 269
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 270
nodes.content: def validate_simple ( data : Any ) -> Literal [ True ]: # always returns True ... type Mode = Literal [ 'r' , 'rb' , 'w' , 'wb' ] def open_helper ( file : str , mode : Mode ) -> str : ... open_helper ( '/some/path' , 'r' ) # Passes type check open_helper ( '/other/path' , 'typo' ) # Error in type checker

nodes.title: Passage 271
nodes.content: Literal[...] cannot be subclassed. At runtime, an arbitrary value is allowed as type argument to Literal[...] , but type checkers may impose restrictions. See PEP 586 for more details about literal types.

nodes.title: Passage 272
nodes.content: Additional details:

nodes.title: Passage 273
nodes.content: The arguments must be literal values and there must be at least one.

nodes.title: Passage 274
nodes.content: Nested Literal types are flattened, e.g.:

nodes.title: Passage 275
nodes.content: assert Literal [ Literal [ 1 , 2 ], 3 ] == Literal [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]

nodes.title: Passage 276
nodes.content: However, this does not apply to Literal types referenced through a type alias, to avoid forcing evaluation of the underlying TypeAliasType :

nodes.title: Passage 277
nodes.content: type A = Literal [ 1 , 2 ] assert Literal [ A , 3 ] != Literal [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]

nodes.title: Passage 278
nodes.content: Redundant arguments are skipped, e.g.:

nodes.title: Passage 279
nodes.content: assert Literal [ 1 , 2 , 1 ] == Literal [ 1 , 2 ]

nodes.title: Passage 280
nodes.content: When comparing literals, the argument order is ignored, e.g.:

nodes.title: Passage 281
nodes.content: assert Literal [ 1 , 2 ] == Literal [ 2 , 1 ]

nodes.title: Passage 282
nodes.content: You cannot subclass or instantiate a Literal .

nodes.title: Passage 283
nodes.content: You cannot write Literal[X][Y] .

nodes.title: Passage 284
nodes.content: Added in version 3.8.

nodes.title: Passage 285
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.9.1: Literal now de-duplicates parameters. Equality comparisons of Literal objects are no longer order dependent. Literal objects will now raise a TypeError exception during equality comparisons if one of their parameters are not hashable .

nodes.title: Passage 287
nodes.content: typing. ClassVar

nodes.title: Passage 288
nodes.content: Special type construct to mark class variables.

nodes.title: Passage 289
nodes.content: As introduced in PEP 526 , a variable annotation wrapped in ClassVar indicates that a given attribute is intended to be used as a class variable and should not be set on instances of that class. Usage:

nodes.title: Passage 290
nodes.content: class Starship : stats : ClassVar [ dict [ str , int ]] = {} # class variable damage : int = 10 # instance variable

nodes.title: Passage 291
nodes.content: ClassVar accepts only types and cannot be further subscribed.

nodes.title: Passage 292
nodes.content: ClassVar is not a class itself, and cannot be used with isinstance() or issubclass() . ClassVar does not change Python runtime behavior, but it can be used by static type checkers. For example, a type checker might flag the following code as an error:

nodes.title: Passage 293
nodes.content: enterprise_d = Starship ( 3000 ) enterprise_d . stats = {} # Error, setting class variable on instance Starship . stats = {} # This is OK

nodes.title: Passage 294
nodes.content: Added in version 3.5.3.

nodes.title: Passage 295
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.13: ClassVar can now be nested in Final and vice versa.

nodes.title: Passage 297
nodes.content: typing. Final

nodes.title: Passage 298
nodes.content: Special typing construct to indicate final names to type checkers.

nodes.title: Passage 299
nodes.content: Final names cannot be reassigned in any scope. Final names declared in class scopes cannot be overridden in subclasses.

nodes.title: Passage 300
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 301
nodes.content: MAX_SIZE : Final = 9000 MAX_SIZE += 1 # Error reported by type checker class Connection : TIMEOUT : Final [ int ] = 10 class FastConnector ( Connection ): TIMEOUT = 1 # Error reported by type checker

nodes.title: Passage 302
nodes.content: There is no runtime checking of these properties. See PEP 591 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 303
nodes.content: Added in version 3.8.

nodes.title: Passage 304
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.13: Final can now be nested in ClassVar and vice versa.

nodes.title: Passage 306
nodes.content: typing. Required

nodes.title: Passage 307
nodes.content: Special typing construct to mark a TypedDict key as required.

nodes.title: Passage 308
nodes.content: This is mainly useful for total=False TypedDicts. See TypedDict and PEP 655 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 309
nodes.content: Added in version 3.11.

nodes.title: Passage 311
nodes.content: typing. NotRequired

nodes.title: Passage 312
nodes.content: Special typing construct to mark a TypedDict key as potentially missing.

nodes.title: Passage 313
nodes.content: See TypedDict and PEP 655 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 314
nodes.content: Added in version 3.11.

nodes.title: Passage 316
nodes.content: typing. ReadOnly

nodes.title: Passage 317
nodes.content: A special typing construct to mark an item of a TypedDict as read-only.

nodes.title: Passage 318
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 319
nodes.content: class Movie ( TypedDict ): title : ReadOnly [ str ] year : int def mutate_movie ( m : Movie ) -> None : m [ "year" ] = 1999 # allowed m [ "title" ] = "The Matrix" # type checker error

nodes.title: Passage 320
nodes.content: There is no runtime checking for this property.

nodes.title: Passage 321
nodes.content: See TypedDict and PEP 705 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 322
nodes.content: Added in version 3.13.

nodes.title: Passage 324
nodes.content: typing. Annotated

nodes.title: Passage 325
nodes.content: Special typing form to add context-specific metadata to an annotation.

nodes.title: Passage 326
nodes.content: Add metadata x to a given type T by using the annotation Annotated[T, x] . Metadata added using Annotated can be used by static analysis tools or at runtime. At runtime, the metadata is stored in a __metadata__ attribute.

nodes.title: Passage 327
nodes.content: If a library or tool encounters an annotation Annotated[T, x] and has no special logic for the metadata, it should ignore the metadata and simply treat the annotation as T . As such, Annotated can be useful for code that wants to use annotations for purposes outside Python’s static typing system.

nodes.title: Passage 328
nodes.content: Using Annotated[T, x] as an annotation still allows for static typechecking of T , as type checkers will simply ignore the metadata x . In this way, Annotated differs from the @no_type_check decorator, which can also be used for adding annotations outside the scope of the typing system, but completely disables typechecking for a function or class.

nodes.title: Passage 329
nodes.content: The responsibility of how to interpret the metadata lies with the tool or library encountering an Annotated annotation. A tool or library encountering an Annotated type can scan through the metadata elements to determine if they are of interest (e.g., using isinstance() ).

nodes.title: Passage 330
nodes.content: Annotated[<type>, <metadata>]

nodes.title: Passage 331
nodes.content: Here is an example of how you might use Annotated to add metadata to type annotations if you were doing range analysis:

nodes.title: Passage 332
nodes.content: @dataclass class ValueRange : lo : int hi : int T1 = Annotated [ int , ValueRange ( - 10 , 5 )] T2 = Annotated [ T1 , ValueRange ( - 20 , 3 )]

nodes.title: Passage 333
nodes.content: The first argument to Annotated must be a valid type. Multiple metadata elements can be supplied as Annotated supports variadic arguments. The order of the metadata elements is preserved and matters for equality checks:

nodes.title: Passage 334
nodes.content: @dataclass class ctype : kind : str a1 = Annotated [ int , ValueRange ( 3 , 10 ), ctype ( "char" )] a2 = Annotated [ int , ctype ( "char" ), ValueRange ( 3 , 10 )] assert a1 != a2 # Order matters

nodes.title: Passage 335
nodes.content: It is up to the tool consuming the annotations to decide whether the client is allowed to add multiple metadata elements to one annotation and how to merge those annotations.

nodes.title: Passage 336
nodes.content: Nested Annotated types are flattened. The order of the metadata elements starts with the innermost annotation:

nodes.title: Passage 337
nodes.content: assert Annotated [ Annotated [ int , ValueRange ( 3 , 10 )], ctype ( "char" )] == Annotated [ int , ValueRange ( 3 , 10 ), ctype ( "char" ) ]

nodes.title: Passage 338
nodes.content: However, this does not apply to Annotated types referenced through a type alias, to avoid forcing evaluation of the underlying TypeAliasType :

nodes.title: Passage 339
nodes.content: type From3To10 [ T ] = Annotated [ T , ValueRange ( 3 , 10 )] assert Annotated [ From3To10 [ int ], ctype ( "char" )] != Annotated [ int , ValueRange ( 3 , 10 ), ctype ( "char" ) ]

nodes.title: Passage 340
nodes.content: Duplicated metadata elements are not removed:

nodes.title: Passage 341
nodes.content: assert Annotated [ int , ValueRange ( 3 , 10 )] != Annotated [ int , ValueRange ( 3 , 10 ), ValueRange ( 3 , 10 ) ]

nodes.title: Passage 342
nodes.content: Annotated can be used with nested and generic aliases:

nodes.title: Passage 343
nodes.content: @dataclass class MaxLen : value : int type Vec [ T ] = Annotated [ list [ tuple [ T , T ]], MaxLen ( 10 )] # When used in a type annotation, a type checker will treat "V" the same as # ``Annotated[list[tuple[int, int]], MaxLen(10)]``: type V = Vec [ int ]

nodes.title: Passage 344
nodes.content: Annotated cannot be used with an unpacked TypeVarTuple :

nodes.title: Passage 345
nodes.content: type Variadic [ * Ts ] = Annotated [ * Ts , Ann1 ] = Annotated [ T1 , T2 , T3 , ... , Ann1 ] # NOT valid

nodes.title: Passage 346
nodes.content: where T1 , T2 , … are TypeVars . This is invalid as only one type should be passed to Annotated.

nodes.title: Passage 347
nodes.content: By default, get_type_hints() strips the metadata from annotations. Pass include_extras=True to have the metadata preserved:

nodes.title: Passage 348
nodes.content: >>> from typing import Annotated , get_type_hints >>> def func ( x : Annotated [ int , "metadata" ]) -> None : pass ... >>> get_type_hints ( func ) {'x': <class 'int'>, 'return': <class 'NoneType'>} >>> get_type_hints ( func , include_extras = True ) {'x': typing.Annotated[int, 'metadata'], 'return': <class 'NoneType'>}

nodes.title: Passage 349
nodes.content: At runtime, the metadata associated with an Annotated type can be retrieved via the __metadata__ attribute:

nodes.title: Passage 350
nodes.content: >>> from typing import Annotated >>> X = Annotated [ int , "very" , "important" , "metadata" ] >>> X typing.Annotated[int, 'very', 'important', 'metadata'] >>> X . __metadata__ ('very', 'important', 'metadata')

nodes.title: Passage 351
nodes.content: If you want to retrieve the original type wrapped by Annotated , use the __origin__ attribute:

nodes.title: Passage 352
nodes.content: >>> from typing import Annotated , get_origin >>> Password = Annotated [ str , "secret" ] >>> Password . __origin__ <class 'str'>

nodes.title: Passage 353
nodes.content: Note that using get_origin() will return Annotated itself:

nodes.title: Passage 354
nodes.content: >>> get_origin ( Password ) typing.Annotated

nodes.content: See also

nodes.content: PEP 593 - Flexible function and variable annotations

nodes.title: Passage 360
nodes.content: typing. TypeIs

nodes.title: Passage 361
nodes.content: Special typing construct for marking user-defined type predicate functions.

nodes.title: Passage 362
nodes.content: TypeIs can be used to annotate the return type of a user-defined type predicate function. TypeIs only accepts a single type argument. At runtime, functions marked this way should return a boolean and take at least one positional argument.

nodes.title: Passage 363
nodes.content: TypeIs aims to benefit type narrowing – a technique used by static type checkers to determine a more precise type of an expression within a program’s code flow. Usually type narrowing is done by analyzing conditional code flow and applying the narrowing to a block of code. The conditional expression here is sometimes referred to as a “type predicate”:

nodes.title: Passage 364
nodes.content: def is_str ( val : str | float ): # "isinstance" type predicate if isinstance ( val , str ): # Type of ``val`` is narrowed to ``str`` ... else : # Else, type of ``val`` is narrowed to ``float``. ...

nodes.title: Passage 365
nodes.content: Sometimes it would be convenient to use a user-defined boolean function as a type predicate. Such a function should use TypeIs[...] or TypeGuard as its return type to alert static type checkers to this intention. TypeIs usually has more intuitive behavior than TypeGuard , but it cannot be used when the input and output types are incompatible (e.g., list[object] to list[int] ) or when the function does not return True for all instances of the narrowed type.

nodes.title: Passage 366
nodes.content: Using -> TypeIs[NarrowedType] tells the static type checker that for a given function:

nodes.title: Passage 367
nodes.content: The return value is a boolean.

nodes.title: Passage 368
nodes.content: If the return value is True , the type of its argument is the intersection of the argument’s original type and NarrowedType .

nodes.title: Passage 369
nodes.content: If the return value is False , the type of its argument is narrowed to exclude NarrowedType .

nodes.title: Passage 370
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 371
nodes.content: from typing import assert_type , final , TypeIs class Parent : pass class Child ( Parent ): pass @final class Unrelated : pass def is_parent ( val : object ) -> TypeIs [ Parent ]: return isinstance ( val , Parent ) def run ( arg : Child | Unrelated ): if is_parent ( arg ): # Type of ``arg`` is narrowed to the intersection # of ``Parent`` and ``Child``, which is equivalent to # ``Child``. assert_type ( arg , Child ) else : # Type of ``arg`` is narrowed to exclude ``Parent``, # so only ``Unrelated`` is left. assert_type ( arg , Unrelated )

nodes.title: Passage 372
nodes.content: The type inside TypeIs must be consistent with the type of the function’s argument; if it is not, static type checkers will raise an error. An incorrectly written TypeIs function can lead to unsound behavior in the type system; it is the user’s responsibility to write such functions in a type-safe manner.

nodes.title: Passage 373
nodes.content: If a TypeIs function is a class or instance method, then the type in TypeIs maps to the type of the second parameter (after cls or self ).

nodes.title: Passage 374
nodes.content: In short, the form def foo(arg: TypeA) -> TypeIs[TypeB]: ... , means that if foo(arg) returns True , then arg is an instance of TypeB , and if it returns False , it is not an instance of TypeB .

nodes.title: Passage 375
nodes.content: TypeIs also works with type variables. For more information, see PEP 742 (Narrowing types with TypeIs ).

nodes.title: Passage 376
nodes.content: Added in version 3.13.

nodes.title: Passage 378
nodes.content: typing. TypeGuard

nodes.title: Passage 379
nodes.content: Special typing construct for marking user-defined type predicate functions.

nodes.title: Passage 380
nodes.content: Type predicate functions are user-defined functions that return whether their argument is an instance of a particular type. TypeGuard works similarly to TypeIs , but has subtly different effects on type checking behavior (see below).

nodes.title: Passage 381
nodes.content: Using -> TypeGuard tells the static type checker that for a given function:

nodes.title: Passage 382
nodes.content: The return value is a boolean.

nodes.title: Passage 383
nodes.content: If the return value is True , the type of its argument is the type inside TypeGuard .

nodes.title: Passage 384
nodes.content: TypeGuard also works with type variables. See PEP 647 for more details.

nodes.title: Passage 385
nodes.content: For example:

nodes.title: Passage 386
nodes.content: def is_str_list ( val : list [ object ]) -> TypeGuard [ list [ str ]]: '''Determines whether all objects in the list are strings''' return all ( isinstance ( x , str ) for x in val ) def func1 ( val : list [ object ]): if is_str_list ( val ): # Type of ``val`` is narrowed to ``list[str]``. print ( " " . join ( val )) else : # Type of ``val`` remains as ``list[object]``. print ( "Not a list of strings!" )

nodes.title: Passage 387
nodes.content: TypeIs and TypeGuard differ in the following ways:

nodes.title: Passage 388
nodes.content: TypeIs requires the narrowed type to be a subtype of the input type, while TypeGuard does not. The main reason is to allow for things like narrowing list[object] to list[str] even though the latter is not a subtype of the former, since list is invariant.

nodes.title: Passage 389
nodes.content: When a TypeGuard function returns True , type checkers narrow the type of the variable to exactly the TypeGuard type. When a TypeIs function returns True , type checkers can infer a more precise type combining the previously known type of the variable with the TypeIs type. (Technically, this is known as an intersection type.)

nodes.title: Passage 390
nodes.content: When a TypeGuard function returns False , type checkers cannot narrow the type of the variable at all. When a TypeIs function returns False , type checkers can narrow the type of the variable to exclude the TypeIs type.

nodes.title: Passage 391
nodes.content: Added in version 3.10.

nodes.title: Passage 393
nodes.content: typing. Unpack

nodes.title: Passage 394
nodes.content: Typing operator to conceptually mark an object as having been unpacked.

nodes.title: Passage 395
nodes.content: For example, using the unpack operator * on a type variable tuple is equivalent to using Unpack to mark the type variable tuple as having been unpacked:

nodes.title: Passage 396
nodes.content: Ts = TypeVarTuple ( 'Ts' ) tup : tuple [ * Ts ] # Effectively does: tup : tuple [ Unpack [ Ts ]]

nodes.title: Passage 397
nodes.content: In fact, Unpack can be used interchangeably with * in the context of typing.TypeVarTuple and builtins.tuple types. You might see Unpack being used explicitly in older versions of Python, where * couldn’t be used in certain places:

nodes.title: Passage 398
nodes.content: # In older versions of Python, TypeVarTuple and Unpack # are located in the `typing_extensions` backports package. from typing_extensions import TypeVarTuple , Unpack Ts = TypeVarTuple ( 'Ts' ) tup : tuple [ * Ts ] # Syntax error on Python <= 3.10! tup : tuple [ Unpack [ Ts ]] # Semantically equivalent, and backwards-compatible

nodes.title: Passage 399
nodes.content: Unpack can also be used along with typing.TypedDict for typing **kwargs in a function signature:

nodes.title: Passage 400
nodes.content: from typing import TypedDict , Unpack class Movie ( TypedDict ): name : str year : int # This function expects two keyword arguments - `name` of type `str` # and `year` of type `int`. def foo ( ** kwargs : Unpack [ Movie ]): ...

nodes.title: Passage 401
nodes.content: See PEP 692 for more details on using Unpack for **kwargs typing.

nodes.title: Passage 402
nodes.content: Added in version 3.11.

nodes.content: Base class for protocol classes.

nodes.title: Passage 619
nodes.content: Protocol classes are defined like this:

nodes.title: Passage 621
nodes.content: Such classes are primarily used with static type checkers that recognize structural subtyping (static duck-typing), for example:

nodes.title: Passage 622

nodes.title: Passage 623
nodes.content: See PEP 544 for more details. Protocol classes decorated with @runtime_checkable (described later) act as simple-minded runtime protocols that check only the presence of given attributes, ignoring their type signatures. Protocol classes without this decorator cannot be used as the second argument to isinstance() or issubclass() .

nodes.title: Passage 626

nodes.title: Passage 627

nodes.title: Passage 628

nodes.title: Passage 630
nodes.content: @ typing. runtime_checkable

nodes.title: Passage 631
nodes.content: Mark a protocol class as a runtime protocol.

nodes.title: Passage 632
nodes.content: Such a protocol can be used with isinstance() and issubclass() . This allows a simple-minded structural check, very similar to “one-trick ponies” in collections.abc such as Iterable . For example:

nodes.title: Passage 633
nodes.content: @runtime_checkable class Closable ( Protocol ): def close ( self ): ... assert isinstance ( open ( '/some/file' ), Closable ) @runtime_checkable class Named ( Protocol ): name : str import threading assert isinstance ( threading . Thread ( name = 'Bob' ), Named )

nodes.title: Passage 634
nodes.content: This decorator raises TypeError when applied to a non-protocol class.

nodes.title: Passage 635
nodes.content: Note

nodes.title: Passage 636
nodes.content: @runtime_checkable will check only the presence of the required methods or attributes, not their type signatures or types. For example, ssl.SSLObject is a class, therefore it passes an issubclass() check against Callable . However, the ssl.SSLObject.__init__ method exists only to raise a TypeError with a more informative message, therefore making it impossible to call (instantiate) ssl.SSLObject .

nodes.title: Passage 637
nodes.content: Note

nodes.title: Passage 638
nodes.content: An isinstance() check against a runtime-checkable protocol can be surprisingly slow compared to an isinstance() check against a non-protocol class. Consider using alternative idioms such as hasattr() calls for structural checks in performance-sensitive code.

nodes.title: Passage 639
nodes.content: Added in version 3.8.

nodes.title: Passage 640
nodes.content: Changed in version 3.12: The internal implementation of isinstance() checks against runtime-checkable protocols now uses inspect.getattr_static() to look up attributes (previously, hasattr() was used). As a result, some objects which used to be considered instances of a runtime-checkable protocol may no longer be considered instances of that protocol on Python 3.12+, and vice versa. Most users are unlikely to be affected by this change.

Monkey-patching attributes onto a runtime-checkable protocol will still work, but will have no impact on isinstance() checks comparing objects to the protocol. nodes.title: Passage 643
nodes.content: class typing. TypedDict ( dict )

nodes.title: Passage 644
nodes.content: Special construct to add type hints to a dictionary. At runtime “ TypedDict instances” are simply dicts .

nodes.title: Passage 645
nodes.content: TypedDict declares a dictionary type that expects all of its instances to have a certain set of keys, where each key is associated with a value of a consistent type. This expectation is not checked at runtime but is only enforced by type checkers. Usage:

nodes.title: Passage 646
nodes.content: class Point2D ( TypedDict ): x : int y : int label : str a : Point2D = { 'x' : 1 , 'y' : 2 , 'label' : 'good' } # OK b : Point2D = { 'z' : 3 , 'label' : 'bad' } # Fails type check assert Point2D ( x = 1 , y = 2 , label = 'first' ) == dict ( x = 1 , y = 2 , label = 'first' )

nodes.title: Passage 647
nodes.content: An alternative way to create a TypedDict is by using function-call syntax. The second argument must be a literal dict :

nodes.title: Passage 648
nodes.content: Point2D = TypedDict ( 'Point2D' , { 'x' : int , 'y' : int , 'label' : str })

nodes.title: Passage 649
nodes.content: This functional syntax allows defining keys which are not valid identifiers , for example because they are keywords or contain hyphens, or when key names must not be mangled like regular private names:

nodes.title: Passage 650
nodes.content: # raises SyntaxError class Point2D ( TypedDict ): in : int # 'in' is a keyword x - y : int # name with hyphens class Definition ( TypedDict ): __schema : str # mangled to `_Definition__schema` # OK, functional syntax Point2D = TypedDict ( 'Point2D' , { 'in' : int , 'x-y' : int }) Definition = TypedDict ( 'Definition' , { '__schema' : str }) # not mangled

nodes.title: Passage 651
nodes.content: By default, all keys must be present in a TypedDict . It is possible to mark individual keys as non-required using NotRequired :

nodes.title: Passage 652
nodes.content: class Point2D ( TypedDict ): x : int y : int label : NotRequired [ str ] # Alternative syntax Point2D = TypedDict ( 'Point2D' , { 'x' : int , 'y' : int , 'label' : NotRequired [ str ]})

nodes.title: Passage 653
nodes.content: This means that a Point2D TypedDict can have the label key omitted.

nodes.title: Passage 654
nodes.content: It is also possible to mark all keys as non-required by default by specifying a totality of False :

nodes.title: Passage 655
nodes.content: class Point2D ( TypedDict , total = False ): x : int y : int # Alternative syntax Point2D = TypedDict ( 'Point2D' , { 'x' : int , 'y' : int }, total = False )

nodes.title: Passage 656
nodes.content: This means that a Point2D TypedDict can have any of the keys omitted. A type checker is only expected to support a literal False or True as the value of the total argument. True is the default, and makes all items defined in the class body required.

nodes.title: Passage 657
nodes.content: Individual keys of a total=False TypedDict can be marked as required using Required :

nodes.title: Passage 658
nodes.content: class Point2D ( TypedDict , total = False ): x : Required [ int ] y : Required [ int ] label : str # Alternative syntax Point2D = TypedDict ( 'Point2D' , { 'x' : Required [ int ], 'y' : Required [ int ], 'label' : str }, total = False )

nodes.title: Passage 659
nodes.content: It is possible for a TypedDict type to inherit from one or more other TypedDict types using the class-based syntax. Usage:

nodes.title: Passage 660
nodes.content: class Point3D ( Point2D ): z : int

nodes.title: Passage 661
nodes.content: Point3D has three items: x , y and z . It is equivalent to this definition:

nodes.title: Passage 662
nodes.content: class Point3D ( TypedDict ): x : int y : int z : int

nodes.title: Passage 663
nodes.content: A TypedDict cannot inherit from a non- TypedDict class, except for Generic . For example:

nodes.title: Passage 664
nodes.content: class X ( TypedDict ): x : int class Y ( TypedDict ): y : int class Z ( object ): pass # A non-TypedDict class class XY ( X , Y ): pass # OK class XZ ( X , Z ): pass # raises TypeError

nodes.content: Ask a static type checker to confirm that a line of code is unreachable.

nodes.title: Passage 751

nodes.title: Passage 803
nodes.content: Decorator for creating overloaded functions and methods.

nodes.title: Passage 804
nodes.content: The @overload decorator allows describing functions and methods that support multiple different combinations of argument types. A series of @overload -decorated definitions must be followed by exactly one non- @overload -decorated definition (for the same function/method).

nodes.title: Passage 805
nodes.content: @overload -decorated definitions are for the benefit of the type checker only, since they will be overwritten by the non- @overload -decorated definition. The non- @overload -decorated definition, meanwhile, will be used at runtime but should be ignored by a type checker. At runtime, calling an @overload -decorated function directly will raise NotImplementedError .

nodes.title: Passage 806
nodes.content: An example of overload that gives a more precise type than can be expressed using a union or a type variable:

nodes.title: Passage 807
nodes.content: @overload def process ( response : None ) -> None : ... @overload def process ( response : int ) -> tuple [ int , str ]: ... @overload def process ( response : bytes ) -> str : ... def process ( response ): ... # actual implementation goes here

nodes.title: Aware and Naive Objects
path: datetime — Basic date and time types

nodes.title: Passage 18
nodes.content: Date and time objects may be categorized as “aware” or “naive” depending on whether or not they include time zone information.
path: datetime — Basic date and time types

nodes.title: Passage 19
nodes.content: With sufficient knowledge of applicable algorithmic and political time adjustments, such as time zone and daylight saving time information, an aware object can locate itself relative to other aware objects. An aware object represents a specific moment in time that is not open to interpretation. [ 1 ]
path: datetime — Basic date and time types

nodes.title: Passage 20
nodes.content: A naive object does not contain enough information to unambiguously locate itself relative to other date/time objects. Whether a naive object represents Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), local time, or time in some other time zone is purely up to the program, just like it is up to the program whether a particular number represents metres, miles, or mass. Naive objects are easy to understand and to work with, at the cost of ignoring some aspects of reality.
path: datetime — Basic date and time types

nodes.title: Passage 21
nodes.content: For applications requiring aware objects, datetime and time objects have an optional time zone information attribute, tzinfo , that can be set to an instance of a subclass of the abstract tzinfo class. These tzinfo objects capture information about the offset from UTC time, the time zone name, and whether daylight saving time is in effect.
path: datetime — Basic date and time types

nodes.title: Passage 22
nodes.content: Only one concrete tzinfo class, the timezone class, is supplied by the datetime module. The timezone class can represent simple time zones with fixed offsets from UTC, such as UTC itself or North American EST and EDT time zones. Supporting time zones at deeper levels of detail is up to the application. The rules for time adjustment across the world are more political than rational, change frequently, and there is no standard suitable for every application aside from UTC.

nodes.title: Passage 737
nodes.content: When DST starts (the “start” line), the local wall clock leaps from 1:59 to 3:00. A wall time of the form 2:MM doesn’t really make sense on that day, so astimezone(Eastern) won’t deliver a result with hour == 2 on the day DST begins. For example, at the Spring forward transition of 2016, we get:

path: datetime — Basic date and time types

nodes.title: Passage 739
nodes.content: When DST ends (the “end” line), there’s a potentially worse problem: there’s an hour that can’t be spelled unambiguously in local wall time: the last hour of daylight time. In Eastern, that’s times of the form 5:MM UTC on the day daylight time ends. The local wall clock leaps from 1:59 (daylight time) back to 1:00 (standard time) again. Local times of the form 1:MM are ambiguous. astimezone() mimics the local clock’s behavior by mapping two adjacent UTC hours into the same local hour then. In the Eastern example, UTC times of the form 5:MM and 6:MM both map to 1:MM when converted to Eastern, but earlier times have the fold attribute set to 0 and the later times have it set to 1. For example, at the Fall back transition of 2016, we get:

nodes.title: Passage 402
nodes.content: Returns one or more subgroups of the match. If there is a single argument, the result is a single string; if there are multiple arguments, the result is a tuple with one item per argument. Without arguments, group1 defaults to zero (the whole match is returned). If a groupN argument is zero, the corresponding return value is the entire matching string; if it is a positive integer, it is the string matching the corresponding parenthesized group. If a group number is negative or larger than the number of groups defined in the pattern, an IndexError exception is raised. If a group is contained in a part of the pattern that did not match, the corresponding result is None . If a group is contained in a part of the pattern that matched multiple times, the last match is returned.

nodes.title: Passage 403
nodes.content: >>> m = re . match ( r "(\w+) (\w+)" , "Isaac Newton, physicist" ) >>> m . group ( 0 ) # The entire match 'Isaac Newton' >>> m . group ( 1 ) # The first parenthesized subgroup. 'Isaac' >>> m . group ( 2 ) # The second parenthesized subgroup. 'Newton' >>> m . group ( 1 , 2 ) # Multiple arguments give us a tuple. ('Isaac', 'Newton')

nodes.title: Passage 463
nodes.content: Suppose you are writing a poker program where a player’s hand is represented as a 5-character string with each character representing a card, “a” for ace, “k” for king, “q” for queen, “j” for jack, “t” for 10, and “2” through “9” representing the card with that value.

nodes.title: Passage 464
nodes.content: To see if a given string is a valid hand, one could do the following:

nodes.title: Passage 465
nodes.content: >>> valid = re . compile ( r "^[a2-9tjqk] {5} $" ) >>> displaymatch ( valid . match ( "akt5q" )) # Valid. "<Match: 'akt5q', groups=()>" >>> displaymatch ( valid . match ( "akt5e" )) # Invalid. >>> displaymatch ( valid . match ( "akt" )) # Invalid. >>> displaymatch ( valid . match ( "727ak" )) # Valid. "<Match: '727ak', groups=()>"

nodes.title: Passage 466
nodes.content: That last hand, "727ak" , contained a pair, or two of the same valued cards. To match this with a regular expression, one could use backreferences as such:

nodes.title: Passage 467
nodes.content: >>> pair = re . compile ( r ".*(.).*\1" ) >>> displaymatch ( pair . match ( "717ak" )) # Pair of 7s. "<Match: '717', groups=('7',)>" >>> displaymatch ( pair . match ( "718ak" )) # No pairs. >>> displaymatch ( pair . match ( "354aa" )) # Pair of aces. "<Match: '354aa', groups=('a',)>"

nodes.title: Passage 468
nodes.content: To find out what card the pair consists of, one could use the group() method of the match object in the following manner:

nodes.title: Passage 469
nodes.content: >>> pair = re . compile ( r ".*(.).*\1" ) >>> pair . match ( "717ak" ) . group ( 1 ) '7' # Error because re.match() returns None, which doesn't have a group() method: >>> pair . match ( "718ak" ) . group ( 1 ) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<pyshell#23>" , line 1 , in <module> re . match ( r ".*(.).*\1" , "718ak" ) . group ( 1 ) AttributeError : 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'group' >>> pair . match ( "354aa" ) . group ( 1 ) 'a'

nodes.title: Passage 483
nodes.content: / usr / sbin / sendmail - 0 errors , 4 warnings
